I have reported the various changes to the investments of each of our entities but it is also noteworthy that in aggregate our Master Trust has increased
$38,237,849 or 3.8% net of distributions for the operations for all of our entities. The Master Trust now stands at $1,050,694,078 as of July 31, 2019.
The breakdown of the Master Trust per entity is as follows:
• Masonic Homes in the amount of $969,683,967 or 92.3%
• California Masonic Foundation in the amount of $36,030,142 or 3.4%
• Acacia Creek in the amount of $23,686,412 or 2.3%
• California Masonic Memorial Temple in the amount of $4,456,944

or 0.4%

• Grand Lodge in the amount of $5,748,645 or 0.5%
• Lodge Investment Program in the amount of $8,177,397 or 0.8%
• Lodge Life Membership Program in the amount of $1,979,013 or 0.2%
• Nob Hill Masonic Center in the amount of $931,558 or 0.1%

The return on investment for the year to date is 4.0% and since inception
of our Master Trust in 1995 it remains at 7.5%.
As we marvel at the size our Master Trust has grown to, we must remember that these funds are not available to simply withdraw to cover all of the
expenses of each of our entities. As I previously mentioned, we are limited to
draw 4.5% of the five-year average of the investments for each entity to support
the operations. This means that in the example of our Masonic Homes with
a current operating budget of approximately $59 million and an investment

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

93

distribution of only approximately $44 million, we have a delta of approximately $15 million dollars that needs to be made up from other sources such
as fees for certain services and each of our annual contributions in fulfillment
of our ongoing obligations to each other.
In 1992 our Grand Lodge created an Endowment Fund to be funded
each year by the budget surpluses of each Grand Master. Since that time
the Endowment Fund has grown to $2,534,115 as of July 31, 2019. It will be
increased once again by the surplus from Most Worshipful Wright. This same
Endowment Fund will now provide $106,412 for the budget of Right Worshipful
Trauner in the fiscal year ending October 31, 2020 compared to the amount of
$104,356 for the current fiscal year.
As previously mentioned, our participation in the Grand Lodge Life
Membership Funds and the Grand Lodge General Investments Fund has
increased over the last year providing lodges a much needed option in their
investment strategies. As of July 31, 2019, we have 51 lodges participating in the
Life Membership Master Fund with a value of $1,979,013 and we have 18 lodges
participating in the Lodge Investments Master Fund with a value of $8,177,397.
Unfortunately, lodges and hall associations continue to experience challenges with budgets, investments, payroll matters, tax filings, real estate matters, and general accounting matters. I encourage all of our lodge officers and
hall association directors to take advantage of the many resources available to
you through our Grand Lodge, including Intacct training, tax preparation services, payroll services, investment guidance, audit guidance, real estate advice,
and many others. In utilizing these services and the expertise of our Grand
Lodge staff, you will be able to focus more of your attention on practicing
Masonry within your lodge and your community.
I would also like to continue to encourage you to begin your budget discussions as early as possible and to include all of the key people in your lodge
like your prospective Wardens, Treasurer, Secretary, trustees, hall association
directors, and those with experience in such matters. Discuss your budgets
openly and frequently so that the finances of your lodge do not become one of
the mysteries of Freemasonry.
Lastly, I would like to thank all of you for the opportunity to continue to
serve you as Grand Treasurer. I truly enjoy working on your behalf with so
many caring and dedicated individuals. I would especially like to thank my
friend, Very Worshipful Allan Casalou. His extensive business knowledge and
passion for our Craft continue to further the best practices and professionalism our Grand Lodge has become well known for amongst our lodges—all for
the benefit of California Masons.
Respectfully submitted,
Arthur L. Salazar Jr., Grand Treasurer

REPORT OF THE
GRAND SECRETARY
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Members of the Grand Lodge:
I am pleased to make this, my 12th report as your Grand Secretary, providing
membership information, progress on our 2020 Fraternity Plan, foreign recognition, and other business.

Membership Information
Current Membership Statistics
As of June 30, 2019, we had 44,815 active Masons, including 2,886 Entered
Apprentice Masons and 865 Fellow Crafts. Nearly 2,000 of these men are
newly initiated, affiliated, or restored Brothers. However, this is offset by 3,213
losses, creating a net loss of roughly 1,300 members. This represents eight percent fewer losses than the previous year, but it lowers our total membership
by three percent since last year.
Our Masonic family also includes 17,228 widows. This year we undertook a full review of every widow record to confirm addresses and other vital
information. More than 14,000 records were updated including several thousand with death information. Widows receive our communications, including
California Freemason magazine. I often receive grateful responses in return. I
encourage every lodge to contact their widows to offer fellowship and support
and keep their records up to date.
Please refer to my written report for detailed membership activity, by-law
amendments, life memberships, and veterans’ awards.
Growth
As I stated last year, the Fraternity’s 53-year membership decline is within
our grasp to turn around. Without sacrificing the quality of our members or
their member experience, there is potential for us to achieve membership stabilization and even growth.

98

Proceedings of the

There are parts of our state that are growing. Forty percent of lodges
initiated more Entered Apprentices this year than last year. Three divisions had overall growth in initiates, namely Division III, Division VIII,
and Division IX.
In the past year, a quarter of our lodges had a net positive growth or no
change in membership. These lodges are located across all of the state, in
urban areas like San Francisco, San Diego and Los Angeles, and more rural
areas like Las Molinas, Hornitos, and Yucca Valley.
Looking Forward
If, next year, every California lodge initiates, affiliates, or restores just
two more brothers and suspends or demits just two fewer brothers, our total
membership should remain essentially the same. From there, we will be in a
solid position for growth.
In 2019, losses due to death were down. Withdrawals were down this
year at 734 compared to 878 in 2018. The most significant losses were due to
suspensions for non-payment of dues, something that we can control. Nearly
1,100 brothers were suspended for nonpayment of dues over the past year –
constituting 84 percent of the net membership decline.
In September, we conducted a survey of all Brothers suspended during
the last two years. The results are instructive. Two-thirds of the respondents
reported that they did not even know they were suspended. Of those who
knew they were suspended, 64 percent said they could not afford their dues
and an additional 28 percent said they had not had any contact with their
lodge in many years. About nine percent thought they had paid their dues. Of
all of the respondents, 82 percent said they would like to be restored to good
standing.
Let’s embrace this issue. Let’s work together to suspend fewer brothers
through enhanced communication and personal outreach and let’s work to
restore these brothers who want to be brought back into our chain of union.
Good progress in this one area could help us achieve stabilization in 2020.
When we created our 2020 Fraternity Plan, we chose to prioritize the quality of the member experience over a numerical gain in brothers. Articulating
this was a cultural shift from the past, and it was a concept born of our belief
that only strong lodges can make engaged Masons, who in turn elevate our
Fraternity and inspire others to follow their example. This must continue to
be our priority as we look towards the future.

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

99

PROGRAMS AND SERVICES
Led by the 2020 Fraternity Plan, the focus of the Grand Lodge office is on providing services to reduce administrative burdens and prioritize the member
experience and needs of the Fraternity. I am proud to say that our Grand
Lodge office has become a true service center for members, lodges, hall associations, and our related entities providing services in administration, finance,
insurance, investment, real estate, legal, communications, technology, education, and training.
Member Services
Our Member Services team provides core support to lodges and members. They processed more than 7,800 service requests this year, an eight percent increase from last year, completing more than 90 percent on the first day
with an average completion time of 150 minutes. They processed nearly 1,500
information requests, and 2,400 awards and recognitions.
Leadership retreat attendance reached nearly 1,100 participants, with 520
officers attending the Master and Wardens Retreats alone. Member Services
administered these and other statewide events, processing more than 3,400
registrations; an eight percent increase over last year.
In 2019, the content of our leadership retreats was prepared by a team
of accomplished lodge leaders to provide tangible strategies for lodge leadership to connect Masons to inspire and mentor one another, and to leave us
energized and excited about what is happening in our Fraternity today. This
Lodge Leadership Subcommittee of the Special Committee on Leadership
Development is headed by Worshipful Brother Paul Dana, together with
Worshipful Brothers Eric Chilson, Marty Cusing, Carlos Diez, Mark McNee,
Mark Nielsen, David Okamoto, Dago Rodriguez, Jeff Schimsky, Gary Silverman,
Chris Smith, and Chris Trueblood. My thanks to these dedicated Brothers for
helping share their experience and leadership.
Lodge Management Certification Program
This year we relaunched the Lodge Management Certification Program—a
series of four online courses, free of charge and written by California Masons
for California Masons to share the knowledge necessary to manage a 21st
century lodge. Since the relaunch of the program in March, more than 3,000

100

Proceedings of the

courses have been completed by members in 92 percent of lodges. Nearly 600
brothers completed all four courses.
Financial Services
The Financial Services team provides accounting, budgeting, reporting,
and audit support for Grand Lodge and our related entities. Additionally, they
provide a variety of supportive programs and resources for lodges and halls.
This year, Financial Services prepared and filed 364 tax returns for lodges,
hall associations, and Masonic Homes residents. Nearly half of all hall associations and almost three-quarters of lodges are now using Intacct.
Lodges not using these services are a minority and some have found themselves with serious financial and tax problems that could have been avoided
if we’d been working more closely together. If your lodge or hall is not using
these services, I strongly encourage you to look closely at the services being
offered and take full advantage of them.
Communications
Our Communications team executes a comprehensive communications
strategy for our Fraternity through websites, social media, email, a monthly
leadership e-newsletter, and California Freemason magazine, which once
again received national awards in the publishing industry, including best
single topic issue for the Sacred Geometry edition.
Nearly 300 lodges and more than 5,000 brothers are regularly using the
lodge app, which connects members on a secure mobile platform. We have
now created websites for more than 100 lodges, as well as halls, providing a
turnkey professional online presence.
This year, Grand Master Wright invited lodges to hold an open house in
September. Our communications team provided marketing support for any
lodge that wanted it. Only 20 lodges took advantage of these services, but
the results were outstanding. Lodges were provided with outdoor signage
designs; print marketing advertisements; Facebook and Instagram advertising; website and email copy; and RSVP forms. The digital campaign for these
lodges alone reached over 790,000 men, left 1.8 million impressions, and the
campaign video was viewed more than 136,000 times. Men aged 25-44 viewed
our video the most. Conversions to open house RSVPs and attendance varied
from lodge to lodge. South Pasadena Lodge No. 290 had the best results. Of
the 4,523 men reached by the digital ads, 159 clicked through, and 60 RSVP’d.
Thirty open house attendees expressed interest in Freemasonry. Simi Valley
Lodge No. 806 and Conejo Valley Lodge No. 807 held a joint open house. Of
the 59 attendees, 12 expressed further interest. Turlock Lodge No. 236 had the
highest attendance with over 100 at their open house.
We hope more lodges take advantage of this program in the future.

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

101

New Lodge Development
Our efforts in new lodge development continue to grow. Three new
lodges were instituted this year, two more are already planned for next year,
and many are preparing to submit letters of intent. New lodges have evolved
in communities that have never had a Masonic lodge, in those where lodges
have closed, and in larger cities where there is rising demand. I will give a full
report on charters tomorrow.
Freemasons Hall
It was my distinct honor to supervise the design and construction of
Freemasons’ Hall, the first meeting place for lodges in this Memorial Temple.
The result is a 21st century lodge hall for 21st century Masons. Inspired by
sacred geometry and ancient architecture, Freemasons’ Hall provides a social,
dining, and fraternal space for intimate, well-connected lodges who desire to
be elevated by Masonry’s rich history and traditions.
Over 60 lodge events have been held in Freemasons’ Hall since it opened
in June. I’m sure you join me in thanking the board of trustees of the California
Masonic Memorial Temple for providing this remarkable gift to our Fraternity!

RECOGNITION OF FOREIGN GRAND LODGES
It is my responsibility to inform the Grand Master of matters pertaining to
foreign grand lodge recognition and to present to you, in the form of a motion,
the recognition of certain grand lodges that meet our criteria.
Mexico
In Mexico, two grand lodges operate on a national or regional basis. Each
of Mexico’s 32 states also has a grand lodge. The state grand lodges participate in a conference called the Confederation of Regular Grand Lodges of the
United States of Mexico, which is similar to our Conference of Grand Masters
of Masons in North America. Our Grand Lodge currently recognizes 15 of
these state grand lodges, and we have received a request for recognition from
one other:
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of the Southwest of the State
of Colima A.F.&A.M was established in 1937. It has 31 lodges and is a
member of the Confederation of Regular Grand Lodge of the United
States of Mexico.
In 2004, the Commission on Information for Recognition
determined that the grand lodges of the Confederation of Regular

102

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodges of the United States of Mexico were regular and met
the standards of recognition. In reviewing their applications, we also
find that they are regular and meet the standards of recognition of
our Grand Lodge.
Therefore, Most Worshipful, I move that the Grand Lodge of California
approve the petitions and grant mutual recognition with the Most Worshipful
Grand Lodge of the of the Southwest of the State of Colima A.F. & A.M. (The
motion was adopted.)
Brazil
In Brazil there is a national grand orient, a separate confederation of 27
state grand lodges, and a number of state grand orients, which are separate
and sovereign from the national grand orient.
Our Grand Lodge currently recognizes The Grand Orient of Brazil and
all 27 state grand lodges. We have received requests for recognition from the
following four state grand orients:
1. The Grand Orient of Mato Grasso do Sol was formed in 1972, has 77
lodges, is a member of the Interamerican Masonic Confederation,
and enjoys mutual recognition with the two other grand lodges in
the same territory whom we recognize.
2. The Grand Orient of Parana was formed in 1952, has 160 lodges, is
a member of the Interamerican Masonic Confederation, and enjoys
mutual recognition with the two other grand lodges in the same
territory whom we recognize.
3. The Grand Orient Paulista (Sao Paulo) was formed in 1981, has 239
lodges, is a member of the Interamerican Masonic Confederation,
and enjoys mutual recognition with the two other grand lodges in
the same territory whom we recognize.
4. The Grand Orient of Santa Catarina was formed in 1950, has 134
lodges, is a member of the Interamerican Masonic Confederation,
and enjoys mutual recognition with the two other grand lodges in
the same territory whom we recognize.
In 2017, the Commission reported that these state grand orients were in
amity with the other grand lodges where they share territory. In reviewing
their applications, we find that they are regular and meet the standards of
recognition of our grand lodge.
Therefore, Most Worshipful, I move that the Grand Lodge of California
extend an offer of mutual recognition to the Grand Orient of Mato Grasso do

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

103

Sol, the Grand Orient Paulista (Sao Paulo), the Grand Orient of Parana, and
the Grand Orient of Santa Catarina. (The motion was adopted.)
Prince Hall
The Grand Lodge of California has requested mutual recognition with all
Prince Hall grand lodges in the U.S. that maintain mutual recognition with a
grand lodge in their jurisdiction that is already recognized by the Grand Lodge
of California. The Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of the State of Florida and the Most
Worshipful Union Grand Lodge A.F.&A.M. of Florida, Belize, Central America
and Jurisdiction, Inc. have entered into an agreement of mutual recognition.
This grand lodge was founded in 1870 and is a member of the Conference of
Grand Masters Prince Hall Masons Inc.
Therefore, Most Worshipful, I move that our Grand Lodge request recognition with the Most Worshipful Union Grand Lodge A.F.&A.M. of Florida,
Belize, Central America and Jurisdiction, Inc. (The motion was adopted.)
Great Priory of America (CBCS)
Concerning membership in Masonic organizations, the California Masonic
Code prohibits a Mason residing in California from being, becoming, or remaining a member of a Masonic organization with activities in California unless the
organization was established or organized in California on September 27, 1957,
or the Constitution and Bylaws of the Masonic organization have been submitted to Grand Lodge for approval at an Annual Communication. Members
of Grand Lodge may submit a resolution to approve the constitution and
bylaws of a Masonic organization, but a resolution is not required. It is not
uncommon for the organization to submit the constitution and bylaws to the
Grand Secretary and the request is made to Grand Lodge in his report.
On July 29, 2019, the Holy Order of Knights Beneficient of the Holy
City, Great Priory of America, also known as CBCS—the initial letters of
the French name of the order—submitted their constitution and requested
approval from our Grand Lodge to hold activities in California. The group
has no separate bylaws.
The CBCS was first established in the 1700s in Europe. The Great Priory
of America was constituted in 1934. A number of California Masons are members. CBCS confers the fourth through sixth degree as practiced by the Great
Priory of Helvetia in their Lodge of St. Andrew and Order of the Interior.
Membership is by invitation only and is limited to 243 members. The constitution is consistent that of other Masonic organizations. Our Grand Master
and Executive Committee reviewed the request at their August meeting and
approved the presentation of it at this Annual Communication.

104

Proceedings of the

Therefore, Most Worshipful, I move that the Grand Lodge of California
approve the Constitution of the Holy Order of Knights Beneficient of the Holy
City, Great Priory of America, and authorize it to have activities in California.
(The motion was adopted.)

APPRECIATION
As I conclude my report, I extend my sincere gratitude to the lodge Secretaries
and Assistant Secretaries whose dedicated work is the backbone of our jurisdiction. I also thank our Assistant Grand Lecturers and District Inspectors
who, in addition to their ritual duties, provide invaluable administrative support throughout the year.
It has been a true pleasure to work with our grand lecturer, Very Worshipful
Brother Ricky Lawler, as he comes to the conclusion of his first term.
I am blessed to continue to work with our Grand Treasurer, Very
Worshipful Brother Art Salazar, who is a great friend and colleague. We are
thankful for the team of true professionals in our Grand Lodge office, all of
whom care deeply about our Fraternity and support our mission with their
dedicated service. I thank them all for their commitment and good work.
Lastly, I want to thank our Grand Master, Most Worshipful Brother Stuart
A. Wright, who has been an inspiration to our Fraternity. While he resolved
a number of difficult issues, our Grand Master has led with a positive frame
of mind. Before he was elected to Grand Lodge leadership, I knew Brother
Wright from his decades of service on the insurance and other committees.
Not only did he bring his talent and expertise to those roles, he always brought
a smile and a laugh and made everyone glad to be with him. He’s the kind of
leader Winston Churchill had in mind when he remarked, “The pessimist sees
the difficulty is every opportunity. The optimist sees the opportunity in every
difficulty.” These personal traits bolstered his leadership this year as he called
upon us to be our best, show our pride for the Square and Compass, and make
a difference. Thank you, Most Worshipful, for your optimism, your inspiration, and your friendship. You truly have made a difference!
And thank you, my Brothers, for the opportunity to serve and work
with you.
Respectfully submitted,
Allan L. Casalou, Grand Secretary

REPORT OF THE
GRAND LECTURER
Most Worshipful and members of the Grand Lodge:
It has been a great honor to serve you this year my Brethren. Our projects
this year have included a continued emphasis towards enhancing our degrees
with music; to the teaching of our Ritual in our lodges; improving degree and
practice planning; and to improving the advancement qualifications process
through the use of our Lodge Management Certification Program.
My opportunities to visit have taken me this year to Arcadia, Pacific
Grove, Santa Rosa, Visalia, and San Diego for the Grand Lecturers Schools in
divisions I, III, V, VII, and IX.
In preparing for each division school, I began the year by asking the
Assistant Grand Lecturers to try and place current and installed lodge officers
from their various division lodges in their respective positions to exemplify
our ritual. This gave us a unique opportunity to observe the quality of the work
and the instruction from throughout the division. I was extremely satisfied
with the quality of the work I observed.
In addition to the Inspectors Ritual Conferences conducted in the north
and south, I made visits to several divisional Inspector Schools of Instruction in
Divisions I, III, IV, and VIII to observe our inspectors exemplify their work for
their Assistant Grand Lecturers. I visited several District Schools of Instruction
and several lodge installations and degrees. I am very appreciative of the hospitality I received from the lodge Brethren at Fort Crook Lodge No. 250 on December
11th, 2018 on the occasion of their stated meeting and installation, and the insightful and meaningful school of instructions I observed while visiting the 240th and
the 907th Masonic Districts. One lodge degree visit stands out for me this year. I
visited Confidence Lodge No. 110 on the occasion of their First Degree ceremony
on February 18th. The lodge Brethren were kind, generous, and considerate to
the candidate and all those who were in attendance. The quality of the beautiful
work was further enhanced by the quality of the beautiful music performed. The
evening was a very memorable one and I thank Worshipful Sigismondi and the
Brethren of Confidence Lodge No. 110 for a very rewarding degree.
We are losing two of our Assistant Grand Lecturers this year who have
chosen, for personal reasons, not to continue.

140

Proceedings of the

Worshipful Matthew W. Ross, Assistant Grand Lecturer in Division V, and
Worshipful Thomas E. Colgan, Assistant Grand Lecturer in Division IX. These
Brothers have exhibited great loyalty and dedication to our beloved Craft.
Please join me in thanking these exemplary Masons for their service to our
Fraternity.
When one door closes, another one opens. I am pleased to report that
Worshipful Robert G. Beeson III has been appointed to serve as Assistant
Grand Lecturer for Division V, and Worshipful John H. Crago III has accepted
his appointment as Assistant Grand Lecturer for Division IX. Congratulations,
my Brethren, and welcome to the Ritual Team.
The 2019 Ritual Competition consisted of the full form Third Degree lecture for both individual and team competition. The Assistant Grand Lecturers
were impressed with the high quality and attention to detail from this year’s
competitors.

2019 Ritual Competition Winners
For the Teams:
From Modesto Lodge No. 206, the ritual team winners for Division IV:
Worshipful Brother Thomas Farrand Worshipful Brother
Charles Heckendorf Jr.
From Channel Islands Lodge No. 214, the ritual team winners for Division V:
Worshipful Brother Wilbert Little and Worshipful Brother Gary Adkinson
From Bellflower Lodge No. 320, the ritual team winners for Division VI:

GRAND CHAPLAIN
INSPIRATIONAL MESSAGE
“Freemasonry, the difference is WHO?”
Today is a day of celebration for our Fraternity. We are all here to honor our
rich history and traditions while both glimpsing into, and helping to shape, the
future with confidence and hope. We gathered here to help make important
decisions, have fellowship, greet our incoming Grand Family, and hear from
our youth leaders, who are the building blocks of our beloved Craft and concordant bodies. In short, we’re here to make a difference.
We’ve all heard our Grand Master’s theme this last year, “…the difference
is you!” But honestly, that seems like a lot of responsibility, right? What exactly
does it mean to “make a difference” anyway? And, if we’re being challenged to
make one, how do we go about doing it?
A year ago, I listened to a Brother, now my dear friend and amazing predecessor, inspire us with his words of encouragement and motivation; honoring
in each of us the multitude of choices in our past and present and reminding
us that those choices shape our futures. As I listened to his artfully crafted
presentation, I thought about the mix of truly amazing Brothers over the last
300 years, who had taken on various roles within our beloved Fraternity. I
thought, “Now those guys, THEY made some differences! They are responsible for young students having books, for kids getting both baseball and life
coaching at camps, for memory care advancements and so much more!”
Everybody at some point in their lives wants to make a “difference”—have
a positive impact on the world that will somehow make it a better place. Being
THE difference is something we all may aspire to in the quiet places in our
hearts where there’s no accountability—where no one will know if we falter,
where no one will judge whether the difference we made was the RIGHT one.
But making a difference is not necessarily the goal we announce out loud in
front of EVERYONE. Even when we step outside of our comfort zone, and
“try” to make a difference, frequently somewhere along the line most of us get
discouraged or complacent. We decide that the BIG changes have to be made
by the BIG people and we don’t see ourselves as “those guys.”
So how DO WE, the rest of us, “make a difference?” I’ve had a year of
watching and learning from amazing people all over California, and the sights

146

Proceedings of the

and experiences along this journey have been enlightening and life changing. Today, I’d like to share an idea about how we go about this “difference”
thing—well, a three-step plan to be exact.
Step One: Show up!
There’s a bumper sticker on my neighbor’s truck that says, “Get Involved!
The world is run by people who show up!” This is where it starts, I think: the
journey to a “difference” starts when we show up.
It’s easy to convince ourselves not to show up. After all, if we don’t show
up, we can’t fail, we can’t be inconsequential. But, when we DO show up, we
pool our thoughts and our energies with others, who fought the same battle in
their heads; the battle about how much EASIER it would be to not show, about
how much we could get done if we didn’t—the battle to convince ourselves
that we are not NEEDED, or that others can “take care of it” and maybe do a
better job.
But, when we persevere and we ARE there, after a rough 8 or 10 or even
14-hour day and still listen actively, and with an open mind; when we are there
because the lodge needs new lights or a clean floor and the only time available
is early on Saturday morning; or when we are there, in a tux, to support the
Brother who is moving up in his degrees, even when the air conditioning isn’t
working; when we are there to support the lodge and families of the Brothers
who have left this world—when we show up for all of this, things start to
change in us and in those around us.
We are THERE to help, to learn, to practice, to support, and to have fellowship with our Brothers and families. But—as so often happens in Masonry—
when we show up, the gifts we receive by just being there in those moments
help us GROW.
This is Step One—because every time you show up—whether the part
you play in the event is large or small; whether the support you offer is a quiet
whisper or a loud cheer; whether you are hero or “hero-support”—in that
moment, life changes and THE DIFFERENCE IS YOU.
Which brings us to:
Step Two: Do what you can, for whoever you can,
for as long as you can.
How can you know how best to make a positive impact now that you’re
“there?” I mean, you showed up, but that doesn’t make things happen. The
point here is that we have a tendency to believe that if we can’t make the BEST
impact, then we must be making NO impact. That’s simply not how it works.
The key isn’t to be the expert, the ONE who saves everything. The key is
to do what YOU can. If you can’t make meetings because of work, but you can

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

147

cook the meat for the lodge family picnic, that’s YOUR impact. If you don’t
know how to rewire the electric, but you CAN steady the ladder, that’s YOUR
impact. If you can’t be the officer’s coach, but you can be a friend or mentor
to the youth orders, that’s YOUR impact. The type or size of the impact isn’t
what makes the difference, it’s the heart behind it.
A favorite story of mine (published by Loren Eisley) goes like this:
“Once upon a time, there was a wise man who used to go to the ocean to
do his writing. He had a habit of walking on the beach before he began his work.
One day, as he was walking along the shore, he looked down the beach and
saw a human figure moving like a dancer. He smiled to himself at the thought
of someone who would dance to the day, and so, he walked faster to catch up.
As he got closer, he noticed that the figure was that of a young man, and
that what he was doing was not dancing at all. The young man was reaching
down to the shore, picking up small objects, and throwing them into the ocean.
He came closer still and called out, “Good morning! May I ask what it is
that you are doing?”
The young man paused, looked up, and replied “Throwing starfish into
the ocean.”
“I must ask, then, why are you throwing starfish into the ocean?” asked
the somewhat startled wise man.
To this, the young man replied, “The sun is up and the tide is going out. If
I don’t throw them in, they’ll die.”
Upon hearing this, the wise man commented, “But, young man, do you
not realize that there are miles and miles of beach and there are starfish all
along every mile? You can’t possibly make a difference!”
At this, the young man bent down, picked up yet another starfish, and
threw it into the ocean. As it met the water, he said, “It made a difference for
that one.”
This is step two: do what you can, because every time you do something
for someone—whether the gesture is large or small; whether it was for a single
person or a large group; whether the time is long or short—in that moment,
life changes because it makes a difference for that one, and THE DIFFERENCE
IS YOU.
At this point, I hope that you are thinking, “Yeah, I CAN do that, I CAN be
there, I can do SOMETHING for a little while at least.” And that brings us to
the most important step:
Step Three: Repeat
Step three is the most important because, as the saying goes, “We are what
we repeatedly do.” When we show up, intending to do what we can, we feel
better—even if just for a short time. We reinforce our bonds to our Fraternity,
to our communities, and to each other.

148

Proceedings of the

Small POSITIVE things, repeated over and over again, become BIG positive things. We become stronger in ourselves, and stronger as Masons. To
borrow the words from a favorite author of our Grand Master, and a Brother
in Masonry, Rudyard Kipling, “… the strength of the Pack is the Wolf, and the
strength of the Wolf is the Pack.”
When we repeatedly do good things, we find ourselves surrounded by
mentors we never knew we wanted, by Brothers we never knew we had, and
by a sense of purpose. We become the strength of the Brotherhood as the
Brotherhood becomes a strength in us.
When you keep showing up, when you keep doing what you can, for as
long as you can, THIS is how we help ourselves be better, THIS is how things
change. And that difference, as our Grand Master has said, really IS YOU!
Respectfully submitted,
David Y. Okamoto, Grand Chaplain

GRAND ORATION
I can vividly recall sitting in the front row of a lodge room in my district,
desperately trying to come up with a topic to speak on, knowing that I would
be called on at any moment to address the crowd. As the Grand Orator, I’ve
become accustomed to speaking at various functions and never having too
difficult a time thinking of the right topic to speak on or what to say. But in
this particular instance, I was asked to speak to a group of DeMolay members
about working in law enforcement.
For those of you who don’t know me, I’m a Captain in the Los Angeles
County Sheriff ’s Department with over 28 years of experience, and in that
time I’ve had some pretty interesting jobs working Gangs, Investigations, and
Patrol in exotic places like Compton, Lynwood, and Firestone; all of which I
could easily speak about for hours. However, at this particular time, I was in
charge of Personnel. Which is to say, I was the HR guy for my department.
How was I going to make that sound cool to a group of eager young men, who
have probably all seen at least a dozen or so police movies and television shows.
I mean, I know what Clint Eastwood would say about Personnel. He’d say,
“Personnel, that’s for …” and you Dirty Harry fans know what comes next. But
I definitely didn’t want to share that with these fine young men.
So, as the last speaker began closing his presentation, I thought to myself,
“What is the thing I look forward to most in my current assignment?” And
it came to me: I love talking to the new recruits, right before they begin the
Academy. You see, I got to give them that talk about what it means to be a
deputy sheriff.
Our Academy classes are pretty large, so I would break the recruits into
groups of 10-15 and sit them around a large table and speak to them. During
my talk, I’d ask them each, “Why do you want to be a deputy sheriff.”
I almost always got some variation of the following responses: “I want
to give back to the community,” “I want to be a positive role model,” “I want to
help people,” “I want to belong to something bigger than myself—an organization with a strong tradition of helping and protecting others,” “I want to impact
lives and make a difference.”
I would commend them all on their responses and tell them, “If you truly
joined for those reasons then I thank you, for those are all noble pursuits.”
I would go on to tell them that this is the greatest job in the world, a sentiment that I would repeat frequently during my talk. I would explain to them

152

Proceedings of the

that I could not give them a job that would make them rich, but I could give
them a job that would give them the opportunity to do all of the things they
talked about.
I told them that as a deputy sheriff they will impact lives on a daily basis
both directly and indirectly. They might pull a person out of a burning car or
home, catch and arrest a dangerous criminal, take a child or woman out of
a home where they are being abused, or solve a cold case murder and bring
closure for a family.
But I would tell them they would also indirectly impact lives as well.
When I would say this, they would stare at me strangely as if I were speaking
in a foreign tongue.
I would tell them that if they believed in the values we taught them, hold
dear to the oath they swore to uphold, and put them into practice each day, they
would impact people’s lives on a daily basis and may never even know they did it.
Now they would look at me even more confused. So, I would tell them this story.
“Not long ago, sitting in the same chairs that you are sitting now, was a
new recruit about to go into the Academy. When asked why he wanted to be a
deputy sheriff, he spoke about how he grew up in the City of Compton, when
it had its own police department and it was very dangerous. The recruit spoke
about his neighborhood being so dangerous that his parents wouldn’t let him
go outside and play.
His parents drove him to school and picked him up each day. When he
wasn’t in school, he had to stay inside his home. In fact, the only time he could
go outside or play in a park was when he was visiting family members who
lived in other cities.
In 2000, the Sheriff ’s Department took over policing the city and increased
the amount of police presence three-fold. All of a sudden, his parents started
seeing patrol cars all over the place, including driving up and down their residential street.
After a while, they started to feel safer and slowly let him play outside in
front of their home. Later, he could walk to school and play in the nearby park
afterwards. At the age of 10, he credited the Sheriff’s Department with giving
him a normal childhood. He made up his mind, at that young age, to become a
deputy sheriff when he grew up.
This meant he had to make some pretty serious life choices. He chose to
stay out of gangs and drugs; get good grades in school and graduate from high
school; go to college and graduate with a bachelor’s degree in criminal justice—the first in his family to do so; apply to the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s
Department and get accepted into the Academy; and finally graduate from the
Academy and become a deputy sheriff.
I am pleased to inform you that he not only did all of those things, but has
now been a deputy sheriff for the past two years and is getting ready to go out
and patrol the same city where he grew up.
Now as a 28-year veteran of the force, I know the only reason a deputy

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

153

sheriff drives down a residential street, without a call for service, is because it
is a slow shift and they are actively looking to try and catch a crime in progress,
before it gets reported.
The funny thing is, those deputies who drove down his street, probably
thought their shift was uneventful and boring, and when they hung up their
gun belts at the end of their shift, probably hoped the next shift would be more
exciting and give them an opportunity to make a difference.
Never realizing the impact they made on the life of this young man by just
doing their basic job of patrolling the neighborhoods. Indirectly, they helped
put this young man on a path that led him to become the very thing they were.
For you see, they were heroes in his eyes when he was a child and now he has
become one too. They made the greatest impact of all and never knew it.”
Traditionally, men join Freemasonry out of a desire to associate with
something ancient, something mythical, something legendary; to associate
with a group that has been the greatest fraternity of men for three centuries;
with a fraternity that is worldwide in its scope, and universal in its welcoming
of all faiths and all races; with a local lodge that helps the family next door
and the school down the street; with a group that was once at the forefront
of issues that shaped this great country and—arguably—was the crucible that
gave birth to the American Revolution, because they were men of action and
social conscience; to associate with a fraternity that claims as its members the
most imaginative minds and the most successful of men.
They come looking for the camaraderie and fellowship that only
Freemasonry can afford. Where men of all walks of life can meet on the level
and enjoy each other’s company and friendship. They want to learn about the
Fraternity and its teachings.
They want to support and participate in the many charitable organizations associated with the Fraternity. They want to use the teachings to become
better versions of themselves. To become better Brothers, better husbands,
better fathers, better sons, and better men.
This still holds true, but there is another reason that men are seeking us
out today. Much like the young recruits I used to speak to before entering the
Academy, many of our new prospects are looking for a way to give back to their
communities and be impactful on the lives they come into contact with. They
want to improve the quality of life for others and make the world around them
a better place to be. Because that’s what we teach: we make good men better
and, in doing so, make the world a better place to live in.
This idea of making a meaningful mark on the world is not necessarily
new. I think on some level we all want to make a lasting impression on the
world and those we care about. We want to be remembered for making a difference and contributing something positive toward society. I think the difference in this current generation of prospects is that they expect it to happen,
and to happen relatively soon—which is not necessarily a bad thing but something we need to keep in mind.

154

Proceedings of the

You see, with today’s technological advancements, this is an age of
instant everything and it is becoming the new norm, especially with those
looking for immediate answers and results. “Siri, what is the meaning of
life?” “Alexa, can you tell me why I am here?” “Oh for God’s sake Matt, just
Google it.”
Now we probably can’t find the answers to those questions, at least not
the real answers, but we do have to acknowledge that there is an awful lot of
information out there and it is as readily accessible as the distance you are to
your smartphone.
If you’ve attended any of the educational retreats Grand Lodge has put
on over the past few years, you’ve probably listened to a TED talk or two with
motivational speaker Simon Sinek. He authored the concept of finding your
“Why.”
He also has an interesting perspective on this current generation and
their need for greater purpose in the world. Again, I caution you that when
a generation is constantly being accused of being self-centered and selfish,
this idea of wanting to do something larger or important for their community
and making a meaningful difference in the world is not a bad thing. It is just
something that we need to be aware of—especially their eagerness and relative timeframe in which they generally want to accomplish it.
Simon says (I love saying that), “Everything you want, you can have
instantaneously…except job satisfaction and strength in relationships. Ain’t
no app for that. They are slow, meandering, uncomfortable, and messy
processes.”
In his line of work, he meets young brilliant people in entry level jobs
and often asks them “How’s it going?” and they respond, “I think I’m going
to quit.” When asked why, they respond along the lines of, “I’m not making
an impact.” This is their answer even if they’ve only been in that job for a few
months.
Simon equates this feeling to standing at the foot of a mountain and staring up at the summit, which represents this abstract concept called impact
that they want to have in the world. What they don’t see is the mountain
before them, which is the journey. What they haven’t learned yet is patience.
Things that really matter like love, job fulfillment, joy, love of life, or self-confidence takes time. The journey is arduous and long and sometimes difficult
and if you don’t ask for help, you will fall off the mountain.
Again, there is nothing wrong with wanting to be impactful. It is, after all,
one of the four main pillars of our 2020 Fraternity Plan, “Making a positive
impact on society.”
Our Fraternity directly impacts society by giving back to those in
need through the California Masonic Charities. Programs like our Masonic
Foundation, Masonic Homes, Raise a Reader, Masons4Mitts, and Masonic
Scholarships benefit our Brothers, our families, and our communities.
Our concordant bodies also directly impact society through their

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

155

charitable foundations—none probably more famous than the Shriners
Hospitals for Children. All together, we Masons work diligently to make a
meaningful difference in the world through our charitable organizations.
But don’t we also indirectly impact society as well as those around us?
Like those deputy sheriffs in Compton, isn’t there something we do every day
without thinking that helps make the world around us just a little better of a
place than it was the day before? Something we might not even think about
or realize?
Masons can indirectly affect the lives of those they come into contact
with and also improve their quality of life by just believing in and putting into
practice, every day, the Masonic values, ideals, and teachings they received in
their degrees.
Harkening back to Simon, he jokingly talks about “Instant Leadership”
training, where you go to a two-day intensive seminar with a bunch of speakers and receive a completion certificate and become an instant leader—but
real leadership takes time. It is a series of small, almost seemingly insignificant things, that when they all add up over time make you an effective leader.
He uses the metaphor of falling in love to illustrate this idea. You meet your
wife, you love your wife now, but can you pin point the exact time when you
fell in love? Probably not, because it wasn’t one significant event that caused
it. It was the small things over time that caused you to fall in love. Being
impactful is, more often than not, the small things done over time that make
the difference:
Like, shaking hands and greeting every Brother at lodge; learning their
names; stopping and listening to their responses when you ask them how
they are doing and actually caring about how they are doing; spending time
getting to know them; and truly helping them with their problems when
you can.
Offering to drive a Brother to lodge, if they can’t get there on their own;
asking an older Brother what lodge was like in years gone by and listening to
his responses; visiting a Brother in the hospital or at home when he hasn’t
been to lodge in a while.
Attending the funeral of a Brother who has passed on, or visiting with the
widow of a Brother who is no longer with us; being truthful; being respectful;
never saying anything negative about another Brother (remembering not to
injure a Brother in his person or good name); helping a Brother when he has
gone astray from these teachings by whispering good counsel in his ear, and
gently admonishing him of his errors.
Brethren, our ritual is filled with teachings on how to properly conduct
ourselves in a manner that will be impactful to the world, if we truly believe
in them and put them into practice. If we treat each other and those around
us with Brotherly Love, Relief, and Truth. If we truly act like Masons, every
minute of every day. Just like the Worshipful Master charged us with in the
Entered Apprentice Degree, ever to walk and act as a just and upright Mason.

156

Proceedings of the

If we support the dignity of our character on all occasions; and strenuously enforce, by precept and example, a steady obedience to the tenets of
Freemasonry, our exemplary conduct will convince the world that the favors
and privileges bestowed upon us by the Fraternity were not undeservedly
bestowed.
Brethren, this idea of making a meaningful difference in the world and
impacting society is entirely consistent with our Grand Master’s theme for
this year, “Freemasonry, the difference is you.”
He envisioned this then as a call to action, inspiring each of us to consider
what we might accomplish when we truly believe in our own capacity to create
lasting change within our personal lives, friendships, Fraternity, and the world
at large.
The difference is you—that is a lesson that is implied in our Fraternity
from the first initiation ritual. What our Grand Master has done is drawn our
attention to it, lest we forget it.
In my lodge, following the initiation of a new member, I conduct a walkabout with him. It’s not ritual, it’s just an informal presentation of some of
the customs and furniture within the lodge and I get to introduce him to the
officers. At the end of my walkabout, I draw his attention to two stones. Both
are Ashlars, one is polished and the other is not. I instruct him to hold the
unpolished Ashlar and to run his hands over it. I tell him that this stone can
be said to represent you; how you are now, in the beginning of your journey,
rough and rugged.
I tell him that each day he will polish his stone, with the lessons he learns
in lodge, to soften out the edges; constantly fine-tuning and perfecting himself
to become a better version of himself.
I then hand him the polished Ashlar. I tell him this is what we saw inside
of him and what we know he can become. I tell him this is the Perfect Ashlar,
that we are all striving for—knowing full well that we will never truly achieve
perfection. I tell him to look closely at the stone and he will see that stone
really isn’t perfect—that, if he looks closely, he will see that there are small
cracks and flaws in it. Because we live in the material world, where nothing is
truly perfect. Only in the Celestial Lodge above, will we ever find perfection.
But that doesn’t stop us, as Masons, from striving each day to be better.
It’s a simple idea really. If I constantly work to be better than I was the
day before, I become a better version of myself in time. Athletes do this
when they practice for sports competitions. Musicians do it when preparing
to perform a symphony. Masons do it with their beliefs and more importantly their actions over time. If I make myself a better Mason, father, friend,
husband, professional, then I will also affect those around me. In doing so,
I improve the quality of life for myself, my loved ones, and those I come in
contact with.
If enough people do it, we can improve the quality of life for everyone
and make this planet a better place to be and life a little bit better than it was

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

157

the day before. Some may call this a dream, but it’s what being a Mason is all
about. Don’t we say, we make good men better?
When all is said and done, what will truly matter most is how much of an
impact we have made as Freemasons on other people’s lives. We will accomplish this not in one large impactful event but in small, seemingly average acts
of kindness throughout our lives: acting as true Masons; constantly polishing
our stones; seeing the mountain before us; embracing the journey.
What a great time to make an impact.
What a great time to make a difference.
What a great time to be alive.
What a great time to be a Mason!
Thank you!
Respectfully submitted,
Matthew Vander Horck, Grand Orator

2019 GRAND LODGE LEGISLATION
GRAND MASTER’S DECISIONS
AND RECOMMENDATIONS

Grand Master Wright’s Recommendation No. 1
Amends the Required Period
to Constitute a New Lodge
Since 2016, our Grand Lodge has instituted nearly 25 new lodges. This
has been an exciting development for our Fraternity and an important strategy
for our future growth and vitality.
Currently, the California Masonic Code requires the Grand Lodge to
constitute a new lodge within 90 days after the issuance of its Charter at the
close of the Annual Communication. Depending on the date of the Annual
Communication, this means the Grand Lodge must constitute the lodge by
mid-January. This requirement has proven difficult to meet given the number
of new lodges. In addition to the national holidays during these winter months,
the Masonic calendar is usually full of installations at this time, limiting the
number of available dates for the constitution ceremony. Most importantly,
the constitution ceremony is an important occasion in the history of these
lodges. It should be scheduled promptly, but it should not be rushed.
Therefore, I recommend that the required timeframe to constitute a new
lodge should change from 90 days to 120 days after the issuance of its Charter
at the close of the Annual Communication.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following change will be made to
Section 801.065 of the Code:
§801.065. ISSUANCE OF CHARTER.
A lodge under dispensation may petition Grand Lodge for a Charter at any
time. The petition shall be considered at the next Annual Communication.
Upon such a petition, Grand Lodge may order the issuance of a Charter to the
lodge, and assign it a name and number on the Grand Lodge registry, if:

162

Proceedings of the

The lodge is found qualified;
The Inspector assigned to the lodge has certified that the Master and
Wardens are qualified to give the work and lectures in the three degrees, have
each received a Certificate of Proficiency in the Candidate’s Lecture of the
Master Mason Degree, and are each proficient in those portions of this Code
that relate to the government of a lodge; and
The lodge is clear of all indebtedness.
The Charter shall be issued as of the closing date of the Annual
Communication at which it was granted. The lodge shall be duly constituted
within 120 90 days after the issuance of its Charter, or its Charter shall be forfeited. Once constituted, the lodge shall be a Masonic lodge for all purposes
and thus shall have all the rights and privileges thereof and be governed by all
the provisions of this Code governing chartered lodges.
If Grand Lodge grants the petition and orders the issuance of a Charter to
the lodge, the lodge’s Dispensation shall be revived and the Grand Secretary
shall return it, together with the bylaws, books of records, and returns to the
lodge which presented them. The lodge may then proceed to work under the
revived dispensation, unless legally revoked, until duly constituted.
If Grand Lodge does not order the issuance of the Charter, it may in the
alternative continue the consideration of the petition one time to the next
Annual Communication, in which event the Dispensation shall be revived and
the Grand Secretary shall return it, together with the bylaws, books of records
and returns to the lodge which presented them. The lodge may then proceed
to work under the revived dispensation, unless legally revoked, until the first
day of the next Annual Communication.
Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee:
The Grand Master recommends amending California Masonic Code, section 801.065 to extend the period for constituting a new lodge from 90 days
to 120 days.
Recently, this Grand Lodge has had the happy task of constituting increasingly larger numbers of new lodges each year. However, the current 90-day
period for constituting those new lodges is proving difficult from a logistics
perspective. If approved, this recommendation would provide the Grand
Master and the Grand Officers an additional 30 days in which to constitute all
the new lodges approved at Annual Communication.
By practice, a lodge continues to work under dispensation until it is officially constituted and physically receives its charter. If approved, this recommendation would not alter that practice.
Recommendation: PASSED

Grand Master Wright’s Recommendation No. 2
Allows Inspector to Approve Change
of Meeting Location, Date, and Time Due to Inclement
Weather or Hazardous Conditions
There are occasions when a lodge cannot hold its stated meeting on
the date or time set forth in its bylaws or at the location previously selected
because inclement weather or non-weather-related unsafe conditions would
subject the members to risk in attending the meeting. The California Masonic
Code presently allows limited changes in meeting dates, times, and location
under certain circumstances. I believe that it is in the interest of Freemasonry
in general to allow a lodge greater freedom to change the time, date, and/or
meeting location when inclement weather or non-weather-related unsafe conditions make it difficult or impossible for members to safely attend the stated
meeting.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 807.000 of the Code would be
amended to read as marked:
§807.000. STATED MEETINGS.
A lodge shall hold a stated meeting for the transaction of business once in each
calendar month, on the date (other than a Sunday) and at the time established
in its bylaws. The foregoing notwithstanding, lodges whose bylaws provide for
meetings fixed by the phase of the moon shall hold a stated meeting for the
transaction of business once in each lunar month, and Mountain Range Lodge
No. 18, Harmony Lodge No. 164, Truckee Lodge No. 200, Big Bear Lodge No.
617 and Rim of the World Lodge No. 711 shall only be required to hold a stated
meeting for the transaction of business once in each of 10 calendar months
during the year, as it may provide in its bylaws.
A lodge may be opened for a stated meeting prior to the time fixed in its
bylaws. However, no business shall be transacted prior to such time.
The Inspector or Grand Master may grant a dispensation to change the
date of a stated meeting, as provided Section 405.060 of this Code.
In the event that the Master of a lodge determines that inclement
weather—including but not limited to ice, snow, and flood conditions—or
non-weather-related unsafe conditions— including but not limited to flood,

164

Proceedings of the

fire, earthquake, civil disturbance and the like—existing on the day established in the bylaws of the lodge for its stated meeting, makes it hazardous
for members of the lodge to attend the meeting, he may, with the concurrence
and consent of the Inspector of the district to which the lodge is assigned,
postpone move the stated meeting to the same day of the week next following
the week scheduled for the Stated Meeting another date, time, and/or safe and
secure location within the same calendar month. The Master shall notify, to
the extent possible, all members of the lodge residing within fifty miles of the
meeting place of the lodge of the date of the postponed stated meeting.
Should a stated meeting be postponed, the business transacted at the
postponed stated meeting shall be limited to the reading of the minutes of
the last stated and subsequent special meetings, action thereon, payment of
the invoices of the lodge, and such other business of an important nature as
determined by the Master to require immediate consideration. No other new
business shall be considered.
Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee:
The Grand Master recommends amending California Masonic Code, section 807.000 to allow a Master of a lodge, with the consent of the District
Inspector, to move the lodge’s stated meeting because of unsafe conditions.
Resolution 18-06 was approved last year and amended the CMC to allow
a stated meeting to be postponed for non-weather conditions. Thus, the CMC
currently allows a stated meeting to be postponed, but only to the same day
of the week later in the month. Fires and earthquakes may make it impossible
for a lodge to meet at their normal location for an extended period of time.
This recommendation would allow a lodge to meet on a different day
of the week and at a safer location. This would satisfy the requirement to
hold a stated meeting and keep the members of the lodge away from unsafe
conditions.
Recommendation: PASSED

Grand Master Wright’s Recommendation No. 3
Allows Grand Master to Exempt Master and Wardens
from Certain Conditions to Installation
The present California Masonic Code requires the Master and
Wardens of all lodges to be proficient in the work and lectures of the degrees
of Masonry as specified before they can be installed. There are occasions in
some lodges where it is difficult to meet these requirements before the installation of officers. While the code provides an extension of time for these officers to qualify, it may be necessary in certain cases to allow a lodge to elect and
install a Master, or a Warden, before he can qualify. It is my recommendation
that these situations be covered by allowing the Grand Master to grant a dispensation allowing the installation of one or more of officers who have not
yet qualified in the usual manner. A Master who is installed by dispensation
without qualifying would not be entitled to the title of Past Master unless and
until he has fulfilled the ritual requirements set forth in Section 805.520.A of
the California Masonic Code.

Recommendations on Dispute Resolution
As I have progressed through the Grand Lodge line, I have been distressed
by the number of disputes resulting in Masonic trials and the time and talent
invested in the trial process. Last March, I asked the members of the Grand
Lodge Committees on Jurisprudence, Trial Review, and Legislative Analysis
for suggestions on how to resolve disputes more expeditiously without compromising due process. They responded. Grand Lodge staff supporting our
dispute resolution process also offered many useful insights and suggestions.
From these suggestions, I offer Recommendations No. 4 through 7.
Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee:
The Grand Master recommends allowing a Master-elect or Warden-elect
to be installed before they qualify in the work and lectures of the degrees of
Masonry, as required in the California Masonic Code, sections 805.520, 805.530
and 805.540. This recommendation would also amend CMC, section 805.020
so that if a Master is elected and installed through this dispensation he would

168

Proceedings of the

not be entitled to the title of Past Master until he has regularly qualified as set
forth in section 805.020(A).
The Inspector of the lodge, with the concurrence of the Assistant Grand
Lecture for the division, would request the Grand Master to grant a dispensation for the exemption.
The Grand Master has advised that some lodges confer few if any degrees
and that it is important to have a Masonic presence in smaller communities. If
the principal officers are sufficiently qualified to conduct the regular business
of the lodge, with the exception of conferring degrees, it may be in the best
interest of California Masonry to make exceptions for those lodges.
The reasoning behind this recommendation is well-intentioned, but in the
long term, are we truly helping these lodges that are having trouble qualifying
their officers, or are we reducing our standards to help a few lodges because
the officers are unable to devote sufficient time to learn the work?
Freemasonry in California differs from several other jurisdictions because
our ritual is performed from memory. Officers’ Coaches, Inspectors, and
Assistant Grand Lecturers—under the supervision of the Grand Lecturer—
dedicate numerous hours of their time to teach our ritual so that our degrees
are meaningful and memorable to the newest members of our Craft. Delivery
of the work from memory has been a basic foundation stone of Masonry in
California and indeed is a big difference between Freemasonry and most
other fraternal organizations. Therefore, if this recommendation is adopted, it
will remain incumbent upon District Inspectors to ensure that only qualified
brothers perform degree work.
Report from the Ritual Committee:
Most Worshipful Wright’s Recommendation No. 3 is a request for an
additional opportunity, by way of dispensation, by allowing the Grand Master
to Exempt a lodge Master and/or Wardens from Certain Conditions to
Installation
There are lodges in our very small rural communities facing unique challenges and have but only a few members who are willing to serve in a leadership role. Most of these brethren are Past Masters from another lodge or from
previous years and are finding it increasingly difficult to meet the proficiency
requirements each year they continue to be asked to serve.
These circumstances are placing the District Inspector in the very difficult
position of making the determination as to whether these brothers are continuing to meet the requirements for proficiency.
Currently the Grand Master may grant dispensations for other lodge functions: formation of a new lodge; balloting for and conferring degrees without
referring application to investigation committee; receiving and acting upon
new applications of rejected applicants for degrees within a shorter period

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

169

than 12 months after rejection; in the event that a Lodge’s meeting place
becomes unsafe or unsuitable for tiled Lodge meetings; the wearing Masonic
Clothing and Masonic Regalia at public meetings, etc. These situations have
one thing in common…the Grand Master is being asked to address a lodge
issue relevant to the lodge in particular and/or to the Grand Lodge in general.
The process of determining whether or not a dispensation should be
granted would be initiated by the lodge leadership, the District Inspector, and
the Assistant Grand Lecturer for the Division for submission to the Grand
Master. This request for dispensation would begin an initial or continual discussion as to the general condition of the lodge. Installation of brethren under
this dispensation would be placed in a similar position as that observed in our
Historic or Research Lodges.
Granting such a dispensation would allow for the leadership and administration of the lodge to continue, bringing further to light the specific challenges faced by the lodge and allowing an opportunity to develop a plan for
the future, without making unnecessary changes to our Ritual and proficiency
requirements.
Recommendation: FAILED

Grand Master Wright’s Recommendation No. 4
Authorizes Pre-Trial Mediation
Mediation is the easiest way to reduce the number of trials. Courts use
them. I am told that the Committee on Jurisprudence periodically initiates a
mediation of the dispute giving rise to charges of un-Masonic conduct before
it for review. I think that we should formalize this procedure in our Code to
encourage its continued use.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 1404.315 of the Code would be
amended to read as marked:
§1404.315. REVIEW OF THE CHARGES BY THE COMMITTEE ON
JURISPRUDENCE.
The Committee on Jurisprudence shall review all charges and specifications
received by the Grand Secretary, strike out those portions of any charge which
are not supported by a clear and precise specification of un-Masonic conduct
and revise those portions of any charge which are incorrect, ambiguous or
insufficient, based on the specifications. The committee may work with the
accuser and the accused during its review. The committee shall append to the
charge or charges a statement setting forth the portion or portions of Section
1401.010 under which each charge is being brought and every essential factual
element of the un-Masonic conduct specified which must be proven at trial in
order for the Accused to be found guilty of that specification. After its review,
the Committee on Jurisprudence shall provide the Grand Secretary with the
charge or charges as they may have been revised by the committee. The Grand
Secretary shall provide the Grand Master with a copy of the charge or charges
as revised by the committee upon receipt.
If in the judgment of the Committee on Jurisprudence any dispute giving
rise to the filing of a charge of un-Masonic conduct before it for review warrants pre-trial mediation, such shall be reported to the Grand Master who may
at his discretion appoint one or more Master Masons to mediate any such
dispute.
If in the judgment of the Committee on Jurisprudence all of the facts set
forth in any of the charges and specifications, if true, would not warrant a
verdict of un-Masonic conduct, then any such charge shall be dismissed by

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

171

it and the committee shall so advise the Grand Secretary. Such a dismissal
shall not prevent any subsequent filing of a charge with more evidence. The
Committee on Jurisprudence shall prepare a written report on its action and
file it with the Grand Secretary. The Grand Secretary shall provide the Grand
Master with a copy upon receipt. The Grand Secretary shall notify the accuser
and the accused of the action taken, as well as the accused’s lodge and the
Inspector assigned to the accused’s lodge. If the accused is a member of more
than one lodge, the notification shall be given to every lodge of which the
accused is a member, as shown in Grand Lodge’s records, and the Inspector
assigned to each such lodge. The Grand Master may at his discretion appoint
one or more Master Masons to mediate any dispute giving rise to the filing
of any dismissed charges of un-Masonic conduct. Alternatively, the Grand
Master may reinstate the dismissed charges as filed if in his view the facts set
forth in any of the charges and specifications, if true, would warrant a verdict
of un-Masonic conduct.
Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The Grand Master recommends allowing mediation of disputes that led
to the filing of a charge of unmasonic conduct prior to trial. Mediation is a
process whereby a neutral third party helps the parties negotiate a settlement.
The parties must willingly agree to the settlement, and no one can force the
parties to agree, or impose conditions without consent. It is routinely used by
private litigants as an alternative to trial. This recommendation is intended
to promote settlement of disputes and reduce the number of Masonic trials.
If this recommendation is approved, then a number of implementation
issues would need to be addressed. Grand lodge would need to develop a
list of qualified mediators and set criteria for their qualifications. Additionally,
policies and procedures for the mediations would need to be created.
Standardized forms for mediations, including binding settlement and release
agreements and reports on mediation outcomes, will also need to be created.
Typically, mediation is an effective and efficient way to resolve certain
disputes. And the Grand Lodge, through its committees, is capable of providing the necessary guidance to make mediations work as an alternative dispute
resolution option.
Report from the Trial Review Committee
The recommendation seeks to formalize the procedure for mediation. It
is the opinion of the Committee on Trial Review that Part 14 of the Code currently appears to limit mediation to situations in which the Committee on
Jurisprudence dismisses charges and the Grand Master may at his discretion

172

Proceedings of the

appoint one or more Master Masons to mediate any dispute giving rise to the
filing of any dismissed charges of un-Masonic conduct. The Code also provides for the Trial Master to explore the possibility of mediation with the parties prior to trial.
Recommendation No. 4 expands the Grand Master’s authority to appoint
mediators, if in the judgment of the Committee on Jurisprudence the dispute
giving rise to the charges of un-Masonic conduct warrants pre-trial mediation.
The Committee on Trial Review supports any measure that expands the use of
mediation to informally resolve Masonic disputes.
Accordingly, the Committee on Trial Review recommends a “yes” vote.
Recommendation: PASSED

Grand Master Wright’s Recommendation No. 5
Allows Certain Trials to Proceed
Without Trial Commissioners
While trial by jury is a fundamental American right, this right is not available in many administrative proceedings. Masonic trials are sometimes more
like administrative proceedings.
At Masonic trials, the jurors are known as commissioners. Under our current law, the accused has the right to be tried by commissioners. If the accused
does not make that election, then the Trial Master is both judge and jury. The
delays incurred and administrative resources consumed in trials by commissioners are extensive. If the potential penalty at trial is limited to reprimand
only, the trial is really more like an administrative proceeding. I believe that in
such circumstances the matter should proceed without the time and expense
of commissioners. The trial record would still go before the Committee on
Trial Review and Grand Lodge to address any improprieties and correct any
miscarriages of justice.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes will be made to
the Code. Section 1404.325 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:
§1404.325. SERVICE OF CHARGES ON THE ACCUSED.
Upon receipt of the Grand Secretary’s notification of the Trial Master’s
appointment with a copy of the charge or charges, the Trial Master shall cause
a true copy of the notification of the Trial Master’s appointment and each such
charge to be served upon the accused together with the following statement,
printed in no less than 12-point type:
You are hereby notified that the enclosed charge or charges of un-Masonic
conduct have been filed against you.
[Alternative 1: If you are found guilty of any charge of un-Masonic conduct, the penalty may be fixed at reprimand in open lodge or suspension or
expulsion from Masonry.]
[Alternative 2: If you are found guilty of any charge of un-Masonic conduct,
the penalty may be fixed at reprimand in open lodge only. You may not be suspended or expelled from Masonry without new charges being filed against you.]
Within 30 days from your receipt of this notice, if personally delivered, or
within 30 days from the date of mailing of this notice to you, you must file with

174

Proceedings of the

the Trial Master a statement in writing that you are either guilty or not guilty of
each charge against you or that you are pleading no contest. If you plead guilty
or no contest or you fail to enter a plea, there will be no trial and you may be
found guilty and a penalty may be imposed without further notification. If you
enter a plea of guilty or no contest, you may submit with your response to this
notice any evidence of mitigating or extenuating circumstances which you wish
the Trial Master to consider in determining the verdict and penalty.
[If Alternative 1 above is used, then include the following: You have the
right to have your trial held before either a Trial Master sitting alone or a Trial
Master sitting with commissioners. You must designate in your statement
whether you request a trial by a Trial Master alone or before a Trial Master
sitting with commissioners. If you fail to make such a designation, the trial
shall be held before a Trial Master sitting alone.]
You have the right to be present at any hearing on this matter. You are
entitled to represent yourself. You also have the right to be represented by
counsel of your choice. Your counsel, if any, must be a Master Mason in good
standing in this jurisdiction but need not be an attorney. You are not entitled
to the appointment of counsel to represent you at lodge expense or to reimbursement of your legal expenses. You are entitled to present any relevant evidence and call witnesses. You are entitled to the issuance of notices to compel
the attendance of Masons to testify at trial. You will be given full opportunity
to cross-examine all witnesses testifying against you.
You must comply with those provisions of Part 14 of the California
Masonic Code applicable to this matter. A copy of Part 14 of the California
Masonic Code is enclosed.
Alternative 1 or Alternative 2 shall be selected jointly by the Trial Master
and a majority of the members of the Committee on Jurisprudence.

Section 1404.620 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:
§1404.620. PENALTIES.
The penalty upon a finding of guilt on one or more specifications shall be fixed
at one of reprimand in open lodge, suspension for a definite period of no more
than one year, suspension for an indefinite period or expulsion, subject to
review by Grand Lodge as provided in Article 9 of this chapter. The penalty
fixed shall also be subject to the following requirements:
Absent mitigating circumstances, the penalty shall be set at expulsion
upon a finding of guilt on one or more specifications involving moral turpitude or the conviction of a crime involving a violation of the moral law;
Absent aggravating circumstances, the penalty shall not be set at expulsion unless there is a finding of guilt on one or more specifications involving
moral turpitude or another violation of the moral law or a conviction under
the criminal laws of the United States or of any other governmental entity;
Absent aggravating or mitigating circumstances, the penalty shall be set at

Absent aggravating circumstances, the penalty shall be set at reprimand in

Involve neither moral turpitude nor another violation of the moral law

governmental entity;
Involve no breach of a fiduciary duty;
Do not involve a knowing refusal to obey the Grand Master’s authority
properly exercised;
Resulted in no material harm to Masonry or any individual; and
Involved conduct not likely to be repeated; and
The penalty upon a finding of guilt on any other specification shall be set
as determined during the proceeding, subject to review by Grand Lodge as
provided in Article 9 of this chapter.; and
The penalty upon a finding of guilt may be set at suspension or expulsion
from Masonry only if the notice sent the accused under Section §1404.325 of this
Code advised that suspension or expulsion from Masonry were possible penalties.
