Grand Master Wright’s Recommendation No. 6
Allows Conviction in Uncontested Matters After Such
Investigation as the Trial Master May Determine
Some trials are uncontested. The accused fails to respond or pleads
guilty or no contest. However, our law still requires the Trial Master
to make a complete investigation. He must review all applicable documents and conduct interviews to determine the guilt or innocence of the
accused. Why shouldn’t the Trial Master in his discretion be allowed to
rely on the charges before him? If the accused wants, he currently has the
right to submit any evidence of mitigating or extenuating circumstances
which he wishes the Trial Master to consider in determining the verdict
and penalty.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes will be made to
the Code. Section 1404.410 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:
§1404.410. PROCEDURE IF THE ACCUSED FAILS TO PLEAD.
If the accused fails, within 30 days as required, to file a statement in writing
containing a plea of guilty, not guilty or no contest, the Trial Master shall,
without further notice to the accused:
Personally make a Ccomplete such investigation, as he shall deem appropriate including, but not limited to, a review of documents and interviews to
gather relevant information as to guilt or innocence of the Accused and the
penalty, if guilty;
Determine whether Assume in his discretion that the charge and specifications are true;
Cause the facts relating thereto to be reduced to writing;
CD. Make a finding as to the guilt or innocence of the accused; and
DE. If the Trial Master makes a finding of guilty, fix the penalty under
Section 1404.620 of this Code. No other penalty may be imposed.
The Trial Master shall prepare a written report of his investigation, the
verdict and the penalty fixed, if any, including the facts upon which he relied
in fixing the penalty. The Trial Master shall sign the written report and provide
a signed copy to the Grand Secretary. The Trial Master shall cause his signed
written report to be made a part of the trial record.

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

177

The Grand Secretary shall notify the accused of the findings and the penalty, if any, fixed by the Trial Master, by certified mail, return receipt requested,
postage prepaid, addressed to the accused’s last known address as shown in
the Grand Lodge’s records. The Grand Secretary shall also notify the accuser,
the accused’s lodge and the Inspector assigned to such lodge of these results.
If the accused is a member of more than one lodge, the Grand Secretary shall
provide notification of these results to every lodge of which the accused is a
member, as shown in Grand Lodge’s records, and the Inspector assigned to
each such lodge.
At the next stated meeting of each constituent lodge receiving the Grand
Secretary’s notification, the Master shall announce the Trial Master’s findings
and the penalty, if any, fixed. The Master shall admonish the members present that the name of the accused, any charge or evidence against him, the
Trial Master’s findings and the penalty imposed may not be disclosed, either
directly or indirectly, to any person not otherwise entitled to the same. The
Secretary shall record in the minutes of the meeting the Trial Master’s findings and the penalty fixed.
If the penalty includes suspension or expulsion, it shall be effective immediately upon the Grand Secretary’s receipt of the Trial Master’s written report
fixing the penalty. The notice to the accused shall include an explanation of his
status as a suspended or an expelled Mason.
If the penalty is reprimand, the Trial Master shall summon the accused
to appear at a stated meeting of any constituent lodge selected by the Trial
Master of which the accused is a member. If the accused is not a member of a
constituent lodge, the Trial Master shall summon the accused to appear at a
stated meeting of any constituent lodge selected by the Trial Master. The Trial
Master or his designee shall deliver the reprimand.

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The Grand Master recommends that the California Masonic Code be
modified to allow a Trial Master more discretion in how to conduct an investigation to consider guilt and penalty in Masonic trials when the accused fails
to respond, pleads guilty or no contest.
Over the last hundred years, how we handle Masonic trials has been
changed from the very strict requirements that all Masonic charges, no matter

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

179

how minor, had to be decided by a trial in front of commissioners from the
accused’s lodge, to today where we only have a trial by commissioners if the
accused pleads not guilty and requests a trial by commissioners.
The CMC currently requires that in cases where the accused pleads no
contest or guilty or fails to enter a plea after being proper served that the Trial
Master shall:
A. Personally, make a complete investigation, as he shall deem appropriate including, but not limited to, a review of documents and interviews to gather relevant information as to guilt or innocence of the
accused and the penalty, if guilty;
B. Determine whether the charge and specifications are true;
C. Cause the facts relating thereto to be reduced to writing;
D. Make a finding as to the guilt or innocence of the accused; and
E. If the Trial Master makes a finding of guilty, fix the penalty under
CMC, section 1404.620.
The Grand Master recommends that we allow convictions in uncontested
matters after such investigation as the Trial Master may determine necessary
in the case. The Grand Master believes that when a brother, properly served
with charges, is not guilty he will enter a plea of not guilty. Therefore, anyone
who fails to enter a plea when properly served is not willing to contest the
matter. Our code currently does not allow any discretion for the Trial Master
when a brother fails to enter a plea or pleads no contest or guilty, he must
conduct a complete investigation and determine guilt and if guilty determine
the penalty. This recommendation if adopted would allow the Trial Master in
uncontested cases to conduct such investigation that he deems necessary to
find the accused guilty and to determine the penalty.
The only concern is in cases where no plea has been received by the deadline. Our code allows the Trial Master to proceed without further notice to the
accused when they fail to respond by the deadline. The problem is our code
allows service by mail to the last known address of the accused. If the brother
is in the hospital or traveling for work or pleasure, he could miss the deadline.
However, the Committee on Trial Review has guidelines for the Trial
Master to use when determining the extent of his investigation in these cases
that resolve this concern.
The Trial Master’s discretion is still subject to the review and oversight of
Grand Lodge and your vote on each trial at the Annual Communication. The
recommendation only gives more options for a Trial Master to complete his
work in uncontested cases.

180

Proceedings of the

Report from the Trial Review Committee
Currently the Code requires that, in the event that the accused fails to
respond or pleads guilty or no contest, the Trial Master personally make a
complete investigation as he deems appropriate including, but not limited to,
a review of documents and interviews to gather relevant information as to
guilt or innocence of the accused and the penalty, if guilty.
Further, in these uncontested matters, the present code requires that the
Trial Master determine if the charges and specifications are true, cause the
facts relating thereto to be reduced to writing, make a finding as to the guilt or
innocence of the accused, and affix the penalty.
The Grand Master’s recommendation proposes that the Trial Master perform such investigation as he shall deem appropriate and that he may determine whether in his discretion the charges and specifications are true.
It is the opinion of the Committee on Trial Review that Grand Master’s
Recommendation No. 6 does not alter the requirements of the Code that the
Trial Master prepare a written report of his investigation, the verdict and the
penalty fixed, if any, including the facts upon which he relied in fixing the penalty. It has not altered the duty of the Trial Master to prepare a trial record for
review of the Committee on Trial Review.
Accordingly, it is the opinion of the Committee on Trial Review that
Grand Master’s Recommendation No. 6 does not substantially alter the duties
and responsibilities of the Trial Master in uncontested matters. Therefore,
this Committee recommends a “yes” vote.
Recommendation: PASSED

Grand Master Wright’s Recommendation No. 7
Increases the Accused’s Participation
in the Pre-Trial Process
Discussions this year on Masonic trials raised two more issues. Under
our law, the accused is notified that charges have been filed against him as
soon as the Grand Secretary receives them. However, the accused does not see
the charges until they have been reviewed by jurisprudence. If you were the
accused, how long would you want to wait until you could read the charges? I
recommend that the accused get the charges as filed with his notice and that
jurisprudence be allowed to talk with the accused about those charges as they
are working through their review of them.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes will be made to
the Code. Section 1404.310 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:
§1404.310. PRESENTATION OF CHARGES.
Any charge of un-Masonic conduct shall be presented to the Grand Secretary.
The Grand Secretary shall provide the Grand Master, and the Committee on
Jurisprudence and the accused with a copy upon receipt. The Grand Secretary
shall notify the Accused, the Master of the accused’s lodge and the Inspector
assigned to the accused’s lodge of the filing of each such charge. If the accused is
a member of more than one lodge, the notification shall be given to the Master
of every lodge of which the accused is a member, as shown in Grand Lodge’s
records, and the Inspector assigned to each such lodge.
Section 1404.315 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:
§1404.315. REVIEW OF THE CHARGES BY THE COMMITTEE
ON JURISPRUDENCE.
The Committee on Jurisprudence shall review all charges and specifications received by the Grand Secretary, strike out those portions of any charge
which are not supported by a clear and precise specification of un-Masonic
conduct and revise those portions of any charge which are incorrect, ambiguous or insufficient, based on the specifications. The committee may work with
the accuser and the accused during its review. The committee shall append

182

Proceedings of the

to the charge or charges a statement setting forth the portion or portions of
Section 1401.010 under which each charge is being brought and every essential
factual element of the un-Masonic conduct specified which must be proven at
trial in order for the accused to be found guilty of that specification. After its
review, the Committee on Jurisprudence shall provide the Grand Secretary
with the charge or charges as they may have been revised by the committee.
The Grand Secretary shall provide the Grand Master with a copy of the charge
or charges as revised by the committee upon receipt.
If in the judgment of the Committee on Jurisprudence all of the facts set
forth in any of the charges and specifications, if true, would not warrant a
verdict of un-Masonic conduct, then any such charge shall be dismissed by
it and the committee shall so advise the Grand Secretary. Such a dismissal
shall not prevent any subsequent filing of a charge with more evidence. The
Committee on Jurisprudence shall prepare a written report on its action and
file it with the Grand Secretary. The Grand Secretary shall provide the Grand
Master with a copy upon receipt. The Grand Secretary shall notify the accuser
and the accused of the action taken, as well as the accused’s lodge and the
Inspector assigned to the accused’s lodge. If the accused is a member of more
than one lodge, the notification shall be given to every lodge of which the
accused is a member, as shown in Grand Lodge’s records, and the Inspector
assigned to each such lodge. The Grand Master may at his discretion appoint
one or more Master Masons to mediate any dispute giving rise to the filing
of any dismissed charges of un-Masonic conduct. Alternatively, the Grand
Master may reinstate the dismissed charges as filed if in his view the facts set
forth in any of the charges and specifications, if true, would warrant a verdict
of un-Masonic conduct.

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

183

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The Grand Master recommends including the accused in a Masonic trial
earlier in the process than is currently provided for in the California Masonic
Code.
Currently, upon receiving written charges, the Grand Secretary is required
to provide a copy of the same to both the Grand Master and the Committee
on Jurisprudence. He is also required to inform the Master and Inspector
of the accused’s lodge that charges were filed. The accused is not entitled
to see the charges until after they have been reviewed by the Committee on
Jurisprudence.
If adopted, this recommendation would require the Grand Secretary to
provide a copy of the charges to the accused at the same time it is provided
to the Grand Master and the Committee on Jurisprudence. At this time, the
Committee on Jurisprudence has not yet conducted a review to determine
which of the allegations actually allege unmasonic conduct.
Currently, before notifying the accused, the Committee on Jurisprudence
reviews the charges, corrects any irregularities, and removes any portions that
are not supported by a precise specification of unmasonic conduct. During
this process, it may consult with the accuser but not the accused. The committee must obtain special permission from the Grand Master if it wants to
consult the accused. If adopted, this recommendation would authorize the
Committee on Jurisprudence to consult with the accused without seeking the
Grand Master’s permission.
This recommendation seeks to address a perceived unfairness in our current process whereby the accused is notified that charges have been filed against
him but is deprived the details of those charges until after the Committee on
Jurisprudence has reviewed them. This recommendation would address this
issue and allow the accused to know the details of the charges at the same time
the Master of his lodge and his Inspector are notified of the charges.
Report from the Trial Review Committee
Currently the Code requires the Grand Secretary to notify the accused
that charges have been filed against him but does not formally provide for the
conveyance of the filed charges to the accused while they are being considered by the Committee on Jurisprudence. Further, while the Committee on
Jurisprudence may work with the accuser during its review of the charges, it
does not expressly permit any communication between the accused and the
committee.

184

Proceedings of the

Recommendation No. 7 would require the Grand Secretary to convey
the formal charges to the accused and further permit the Committee on
Jurisprudence to communicate with the accused while continuing to work
with the accuser. It would continue to protect the accused to the extent that
no communication between the Committee on Jurisprudence and the accused
or the accuser in connection with the committee’s review of the charges can
be used by anyone as evidence at trial.
It is the opinion of the Committee on Trial Review that Recommendation
No. 7 allows for the transparency of the process at the earliest opportunity and
may improve the chances of early resolution of the matter through mediation.
Accordingly, the Committee on Trial Review recommends a “yes” vote on
Recommendation No. 7.
Recommendation: PASSED

Resolution No. 18-04
Removes Restrictions on Holding
A Tiled Meeting on A Sunday
The proponents of this resolution seek to remove restrictions on conferring degrees and/or holding a stated or tiled special meeting on a Sunday.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, by definition, California Freemasonry does not require a member
to be a Christian, only that he profess his belief in a Supreme Being and a
future existence; and
WHEREAS, men of different faiths with different days of worship are members of our great fraternal body, so how can we favor one person’s Sabbath
observation over another if we truly consider every man and his faith to be
equal; and
WHEREAS, there are concordant bodies that require its members practice
Christianity that hold their tiled meetings and degrees on Sundays, so it is
logical that the symbolic or blue lodges who do not have Christianity as a prerequisite should not have a restriction against meeting on Sundays; and
WHEREAS, the time restraints of today’s young masons are far different that
those of our fathers and grandfathers; and
WHEREAS, lodges of young members with demanding employment and
family obligations need the flexibility to meet at a time that is most practical
for the majority of its members; and
WHEREAS, removing the Sunday restriction allows more flexibility when
scheduling lodge meetings and degrees.

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The proponents of this legislation wish to remove the restriction on conferring degrees or holding tiled meetings on Sunday. The Grand Lodge of
California was formed nearly 170 years ago. It was formed by Mason who were
primarily Christian. As such, Sunday was reserved as a day of worship.
California Masonry does not require a man to be of any particular religion.
We only require that he believes in a Supreme Being and future existence.
While the majority of the members of the fraternity are Christian, we have
embraced members from a vast array of religions. This has strengthened our
fraternity in many ways. Many of these religions have a Holy day other than
Sunday, or no specific Holy day day at all. California Masonry is very accepting
of different cultures and religious beliefs.
Time is a precious commodity. Having the flexibility to hold meetings and
degrees at a time that is convenient for the members of the Lodge is extremely
important. Removing this restriction would give Lodges the option to expand
their calendars.
This legislation, if adopted, would remove a bias in our law towards a specific religious belief. That would lead to a more inclusive organization.
Resolution: PASSED

Finally, my Brethren, as this association has been formed
and perfected in so much unanimity and concord, so may
it long continue. May you long enjoy every satisfaction and
delight which friendship can afford. May kindness and brotherly affection distinguish your conduct as men and as Masons.
Within your peaceful walls may your children’s children
celebrate with joy and gratitude, the annual recurrence of this
auspicious solemnity. And may the tenets of our profession
be transmitted through this lodge, pure and unimpaired, from
generation to generation.
The lodge Wardens and members may be seated.
Masters, who remain standing, again turn to face the I.O. for
gavel presentation.

194

Proceedings of the

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
This resolution states it is the intent of the proponents to provide the
option, during the annual Installation Ceremony, of having all the members of
a Lodge rise when the Installing Officer addresses them. However, as written,
this change would not be optional; it would be required.
Currently, the Installing Officer addresses the members while they remain
seated. The proponents believe there is value in including the members in the
ceremony by having them stand as they are reminded of their duties to the
Lodge.
It should be noted that the annual Installation Ceremony is part of the
Ritual. It has been the custom of the Grand Lodge of California to not make
changes to the Ritual, unless there are compelling reasons to do so. It is up to
the voting Membership of this Grand Lodge to decide if there are compelling
reasons to adopt this change.
Report from the Ritual Committee
The proponents of Resolution 2018-05 seek to modify the Installation
Ritual for ceremony for Constituent Lodges to allow the Installing Officer to
gavel the brethren of the lodge up prior to giving the lodge membership
present their instructions.
The Master is given his admonitions while standing in front of the east
to convey the importance of the instructions given by the Installing Officer
relative to the Master’s actions and attitude towards peace and harmony, and
placing the will and pleasure of the lodge as a whole, above his own.
The Wardens are given their instructions in like manner. Their instructions are equally important to assisting the Master in the government of the
lodge and in their readiness to serve in the Master’s absence.
The gaveling up of the brethren instills the importance of the instructions that is not adequately conveyed while the brethren remained seated. The
250 Proceedings of the words of instruction given to the standing members of
the lodge conveys a sense of responsibility to the brethren that they are just
as responsible for the keeping of the peace and harmony of the lodge as the
Master and Wardens are charged to do.
This resolution does not take anything from the Ritual of the installation.
On the contrary, it enhances our Installation Ritual and gives more meaning to
it. The Ritual Committee is unanimous in urging a YES vote.
Resolution: PASSED

Resolution No. 19-01
Permits Calling Up at Stated
Meetings for Masonic Education
The proponents of this resolution seek to allow the presentation of Masonic
education materials suitable only for Fellow Crafts and Master Masons in a
lodge of Entered Apprentice Masons
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Masonic education for Fellow Crafts and Master Masons is
important for their understanding of Freemasonry; and
WHEREAS, it is important from time to time to offer such Masonic Education
to Fellow Crafts and Master Masons on the same evening as the stated meeting; and
WHEREAS, our present law only provides for the raising of an Entered
Apprentice lodge at a stated meeting to a higher degree for the purpose of
examination of candidates; and
WHEREAS, it would be useful if the Entered Apprentice lodge at a stated
meeting could also be raised to a higher degree from time to time for Masonic
education of Fellow Crafts and Master Masons in the esoteric symbolism of
Freemasonry pertaining to those degrees.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 807.020.A of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
Work to be Done in Lodge of Entered Apprentice Masons. All business,
except examinations in the Candidate’s Lecture of the Fellow Craft and
Master Mason degrees, the conferring of the Fellow Craft and Master
Mason degrees, the presentation of Masonic education materials suitable
only for Fellow Crafts and Master Masons, and the consideration of relief

196

Proceedings of the
of a worthy Mason, shall be done in a lodge of Entered Apprentice Masons.
At the option of the retiring Master, the lodge may be opened either on the
First Degree or on the Third Degree for the purpose of installing officers.
A lodge of Master Masons may be called down for examinations in the
Candidate’s Lecture of the Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft degrees.
A lodge of Fellow Craft Masons may be called down for examinations in
the Candidate’s Lecture of the Entered Apprentice degree. At a stated
meeting, the lodge may be called up for examinations in the Candidate’s
Lecture of the Fellow Craft and Master Mason degrees, or for purposes of
Masonic education.

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee:
The proponents of this resolution wish to increase the times that a Lodge
may call up to a higher degree. Since the adoption of Resolution 11-06, all
Lodge business has been conducted in the Entered Apprentice Degree. That
resolution allowed for the calling down from a higher degree but did not allow
calling up from a lower degree except for candidate examinations.
Masonic education is essential to increasing a Mason’s understanding of
the history and symbolism within the fraternity. There are topics of education
that are applicable to only Fellow Craft and Master Masons. This education
therefore must be presented in a Lodge of the appropriate Degree. The current
code does not limit the number or Degree of Lodge special meetings. There
are instances where it could be more beneficial to the members of a Lodge
to receive this education at a Stated Meeting. Scheduling in today’s hectic
lifestyle means decisions must be made as to where to spend available time.
Many members only have the time to attend the Lodge’s Stated Meeting. They
would therefore miss any education conducted at a special meeting.
This resolution would give the Master of the Lodge the option of calling
up his Lodge, for the purpose of Masonic education.
Resolution: PASSED

Resolution No. 19-02:
Allows Masonic Membership
with Single Conviction
The proponents of this resolution seek to allow Masonic membership for
men convicted of a single crime more than five years in the past.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, our fraternity takes good men and makes them better; and
WHEREAS, there are some men who seek membership who have made poor
decisions in the distant past, either as juveniles or as very young adults, and
who have now been rehabilitated; and
WHEREAS, these rehabilitated men possess proof of their rehabilitation via
court records establishing offense expungement and/or many years without
another offense; and
WHEREAS, there are, in fact, rehabilitated and now good men who deserve a
second chance to become better men via our fraternity so they can give back
to their community in general and to their lodge, should they be admitted, in
particular; and
WHEREAS, our California Masonic Code allows brethren who have been
expelled for minor law violations to be readmitted to the fraternity upon showing proof of rehabilitation, the same compassion should be extended toward
applicants who also show proof of rehabilitation and are now good men.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 804.210 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§804.210. CRIMINAL RECORD.
No person shall hold or be eligible for membership in any constituent lodge who has pleaded guilty or nolo contendere to, or has been
convicted of, a crime involving a violation of the moral law unless:

198

Proceedings of the

For the reason that he did not commit the offense, he either has been
pardoned or had his judgment of conviction vacated or reversed; or
A single such plea or conviction has been identified and he has had
his conviction expunged under California Penal Code
Section 1203.4 or a comparable provision in the jurisdiction of the
conviction.
The Grand Secretary shall make available to constituent lodges a
service reasonably designed to verify compliance with the foregoing
requirements of this section in a cost-effective manner. The fee for
this service shall be established from time to time with the adoption
of the Grand Lodge budget.
Each constituent lodge shall use this service to verify compliance by
each of its applicants for the degrees and by each of its applicants
for affiliation whose demit or certificate is from a lodge in another
Jurisdiction. Each such applicant shall contribute the fee for this
service with his application, and such fee shall be nonrefundable.
Each constituent lodge at its discretion and at its own expense may
use this service to verify compliance by any of its other applicants for
affiliation or by any Mason of such lodge.
If compliance verification discloses information that an applicant
is ineligible for the degrees because he has pled guilty or no contest
to, or has been convicted of, a crime of moral turpitude, the Grand
Secretary shall immediately review and confirm the information.
His confirmation shall have the same effect as the application being
rejected, except that such applicant shall not have the opportunity
to apply for membership until a minimum of five years has elapsed
since the date of such crime again at any future time unless, for
the reason that he did not commit the offense, he either has been
pardoned or had his judgment of conviction vacated or reversed. A
letter shall be sent to such applicant by the Grand Secretary informing him of the information that was obtained, his current status as an
applicant, and the procedure to appeal the information if he believes
that it is incorrect. Any appeal shall be resolved by a majority of the
members of the Committee on Jurisprudence. The lodge Secretary
shall be advised of the action taken. If no criminal history is discovered, the Lodge Secretary shall be so informed.
If compliance verification discloses information that an applicant
is ineligible for the degrees because he has pled guilty or no contest
to, or has been convicted of, a crime or crimes which If a criminal

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

199

history is discovered, but the crime or crimes do not involve moral
turpitude, the information shall be sent to the lodge to determine
whether the crime or crimes involve a violation of the moral law. If
the lodge makes that determination, such determination shall have
the same effect as the application being rejected. Unless the applicant has clearly violated the moral law by committing a crime involving moral turpitude, the lodge shall determine in the exercise of its
sound discretion whether the applicant’s criminal record disqualifies
him from receiving the degrees.
Whether a Mason with a criminal history (however discovered)
remains eligible for the rights and privileges of Masonry as a result of
that history shall be addressed as provided in Part 14 of this code.
It is the duty of every Mason to maintain the confidentiality of any
matters arising under this section. Nothing about any matter arising
under this section may be disclosed, either directly or indirectly, to
any person other than a member of a constituent lodge or as otherwise authorized in this code or by the Grand Master. Unless otherwise authorized by Grand Lodge or the Grand Master, nothing about
any matter arising under this section shall be published beyond the
notifications provided in this section. Every written notification provided in this section shall include a reminder of the confidentiality
requirements of this section.
Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The proponents seek to amend California Masonic Code, section 804.210
to allow Masonic membership for men convicted of a single crime more than
five years in the past. The proponents contend men who may have made
poor decisions in the distant past may now be rehabilitated and worthy of
membership.
The CMC currently renders ineligible for membership anyone who has
been convicted of, or has pleaded guilty or no contest to, a crime involving a
violation of the moral law. This prohibition does not apply if—for the reason
that he did not commit the offense—the conviction was pardoned, vacated, or
reversed. And even then, Grand Lodge must approve the application.
This resolution would create a new exception for applicants who have
been convicted of, or have pleaded guilty or no contest to, a crime involving a
violation of the moral law. This exception would apply when there is only one
crime and it has been expunged under California Penal Code, section 1203.4,
or a similar law if the crime was committed outside California. In contrast to
current requirements for those who are pardoned, vacated, or reversed, Grand
Lodge (this voting body) would have no say.

200

Proceedings of the

Penal Code, section 1203.4 allows a person to petition a court to have his
conviction or plea expunged. To be eligible, the petitioner must have fulfilled
all conditions of probation for the entire probationary period, not be currently
incarcerated, and not charged with a new crime. If the petition is granted, the
conviction or plea is set aside, the court dismisses the accusations, and the
petitioner is released from nearly all penalties and disabilities resulting from
the crime.
Not all crimes can be expunged in California. Crimes that result in serving
time in state prison cannot be expunged. Also, crimes under the umbrella of
child molestation, child pornography, and rape are categorically ineligible for
expungement under Penal Code, section 1203.4.
Also of note, not all penalties imposed by conviction or plea are reversed
by section 1203.4. Expungement does not affect restrictions on owning, possessing, or having custody of firearms if those restrictions were the result of
the conviction or plea. It does not affect the suspension or revocation of a
driver license resulting from the conviction or plea. It does not affect a prohibition from holding public office resulting from the conviction or plea. And it
does not affect one’s registration as a sex offender.
If adopted, this resolution would allow a first-time applicant with a single
conviction that has already been expunged to apply for degrees. But if the
applicant has not yet had his single conviction expunged, then this resolution
would allow him to reapply after he has both waited five years from the date of
the crime and had his conviction expunged.
This resolution would represent a significant change in how this Grand
Lodge treats applicants with convictions and pleas for crimes involving violations of the moral law. Currently, only applicants who were determined to
have not committed the offense and subsequently pardoned or had the conviction vacated or reversed are allowed to be considered for membership. This
resolution would allow for consideration for membership, applicants who
have committed the offense, and even those who admitted guilt, without any
oversight by the voting delegates of Grand Lodge.
Resolution: FAILED

Resolution No. 19-03:
Increases Refreshment Revolving Fund
The proponents of this resolution seek to increase the Refreshment fund to
$1,000.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, it is the custom and duty of the Junior Warden or Stewards to
provide for the refreshments for the Craft; and
WHEREAS, the amount authorized in the Masonic code for the refreshment
revolving fund has not been increased in the last two decade; and
WHEREAS, inflation has not been stagnant over the last two decades; and
WHEREAS, the amount for the refreshment fund should be increased to
$1000.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 809.120 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§809.120. LODGE REVOLVING FUNDS.
A lodge may establish two revolving funds. One such fund, consisting
of not more than $1,000$500, may be established for the use of its
Stewards or Junior Warden, as the Master may determine, in providing
refreshments for all regular lodge functions. One such fund, consisting
of not more than $500, may be established for the use of its Secretary
for his incidental expenses. Each such revolving fund may be replenished
monthly on presentation of receipted vouchers and shall remain subject
to provisions of this code.
Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee:
The proponents of this resolution wish to increase the maximum amount
of the refreshment fund from $500 to $1,000 by amending Section 809.120 of

202

Proceedings of the

the California Masonic Code. They do not propose to change the Secretaries
fund. The proponent stated that his Lodge regularly spends $900 to $1,200
from the refreshment fund every month. This places a burden on the Stewards
or Junior Warden making the purchases each month to use their own money to
purchase refreshments. They point out that the fund has not been increased
in the last 20 years, while inflation has reduced the purchasing power of the
$500 fund.
The creation of the optional revolving funds described in Section 809.120
began as Grand Master Leo A. Andersion’s Decision #17 in 1958. His decision was presented to Grand Lodge who by a 5/6ths voted created an optional
revolving fund for Stewards and set the limit at $100. In 1958 a resolution
added the Junior Warden to the officers who could use the optional fund. Over
the years, another optional revolving fund was approved for the secretary set
at the same amount for Stewards or Junior Warden. Those amounts were later
changed to $250 for refreshments and $100 for the secretary. Finally, in 1990,
Resolution 90-18, increased both optional funds to $500 and there have been
no changes since then.
Applying the cost of living index since 1990 to the $500, it would take a
little more than $979.69 in 2019 dollars to have same buying power. The purpose of the optional funds is to make it easier for Stewards and/or the Junior
Warden to pay for necessary supplies without creating a burden by using their
own money. It would still be up to each lodge to determine if they have a fund
and how much their lodge’s revolving fund will be, the resolution would only
raise the maximum to $1,000.
This resolution would bring the revolving refreshment fund’s maximum
purchasing power back to within $20 of the level approved in 1990.
Resolution: PASSED

Resolution No. 19-04:
Allows Option to Compensate Treasurer
The proponents of this resolution seek to allow a lodge the option to compensate its Treasurer.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the Treasurer’s duties involve certain accounting and bookkeeping skills; and
WHEREAS, maintenance of lodge financial records may require significant
time and effort; and
WHEREAS, frequent reporting of lodge financial activity and status is important for lodge security; and
WHEREAS, the level of effort required of Treasurers varies from lodge to
lodge, the determination of payment should therefore be discretionary.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 805.030 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§805.030. COMPENSATION.
No lodge officer may receive compensation for his services as such,
except as provided in Sections 805.220, 805.230, 805.320, 805.330 and
809.550.F of this code.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 805.220 of the California Masonic
Code be amended as marked:
§805.220. DUTIES OF TREASURER.
It shall be the duty of the Treasurer to:
A. Receive all monies from the Secretary and shall keep an accurate and
just account thereof, giving his receipt therefor, and shall pay the same

204

Proceedings of the

out only when an order is duly signed by the Master, countersigned by
the Secretary, and approved by vote of the lodge;
B. Safely keep all monies, property and other assets of the lodge, except
to the extent they are entrusted to the lodge trustees by resolution,
disburse or transfer the same, or any part thereof, upon the order of the
Master, duly attested by the Secretary with the approval of the lodge;
C. Keep a book or books wherein a correct account of his receipts and
disbursements shall be exhibited in detail, accounting for sources of
income and expenditures, and all monies, property and other assets of
the Lodge;
D. Present to the lodge at each stated meeting in August a comprehensive
statement of the lodge’s income and expenditures, assets and liability, on
a form promulgated by the Grand Master, for the six month period ending
on the preceding June 30th and present at each February stated meeting
a similar statement for the twelve month period ending on the preceding
December 31st; and
E. Perform such other duties, appertaining to his office, as the bylaws of
the lodge or this code may require or the lodge may direct.
The Treasurer shall receive such compensation for his services as the
lodge may direct.
The lodge may at any time when considered necessary cause the
Treasurer to present an account of his receipts and disbursements, and
of monies, property and other assets of the lodge on hand.
Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The proponents of this resolution seek to permit a Lodge to compensate its Treasurer. This Grand Lodge last considered this issue in 2011 with
Resolution 11-04, which failed.
The California Masonic Code currently does not permit a Lodge to compensate its officers other than its Secretary, Assistant Secretary, Organist, and
Tiler. The duties of those officers, which a Lodge is permitted to compensate,
are time-consuming and/or require special skills or knowledge. As a result, a
Lodge is permitted to compensate those officers in order to attract Masons
with the requisite time, skillsets and knowledge to serve in those offices and
to retain them.
The duties of a Lodge Treasurer are numerous and include the receipt of
monies, the maintenance of the Lodge’s financial books and records, financial

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

205

reporting, and preparing (or assisting in preparing) the Lodge’s tax returns.
While some Lodges use the financial services available through Grand Lodge
to assist the Treasurer with his duties, other Lodges do not. It can be reasonably argued that a Lodge Treasurer’s duties are as demanding, and require
skills as specialized, as those of the Lodge officers that may receive compensation under the current CMC, and that permitting a Lodge to compensate
its Treasurer can help the Lodge attract and retain Masons with the requisite
talent and time to the office of Treasurer.
Under this resolution, the Treasurer would only be entitled to such compensation as the Lodge may direct. Accordingly, this resolution does not
require a Lodge to compensate its Treasurer; it gives a Lodge the option to
do so and the amount of the Treasurer’s compensation would still need to be
considered and voted upon by the Lodge’s members.
If a Lodge opts to compensate its Treasurer, the Lodge would need to
comply with applicable Federal and state employment requirements, including the withholding of taxes and the provision of worker’s compensation
insurance. Likewise, the Lodge should take steps to ensure proper oversight
and auditing of the Treasurer’s actions, particularly where a Lodge does not
use a third party payroll service to pay its employees.
Resolution: PASSED

Resolution No. 19-05:
Requires Disclosure Why a Member
is Excluded from a Meeting
The proponents of this resolution seek to require the Master to state and
the Secretary to record in the minutes why any member of the lodge has been
excluded from or refused admission to that lodge meeting.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, CMC Section 804.440 states in part that every member of a lodge
in good standing when present must vote upon a ballot; and
WHEREAS, CMC Section 804.815 states in part that it is the right of every
member of a lodge at all times to be present and participate in its proceedings
while he conducts himself with due order and propriety; and
WHEREAS, CMC Section 804.815 also states that if there is a breach of propriety, the Master may refuse a member admission or exclude him; and
WHEREAS, a Master could abuse this discretion to sway a ballot.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 804.815 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§804.815. RIGHT TO ATTEND MEETINGS.
Except as otherwise provided in Section 807.020 of this code, it is
the right of every member of a lodge at all times to be present and
participate in its proceedings while he conducts himself with due
order and propriety. For a breach of propriety, the Master may refuse
him admission or exclude him. The Master should refuse admission
to any member who presents himself in a state of intoxication. The
Master shall state and the Secretary shall record in the minutes why
any member of the lodge has been excluded from or refused admission to that lodge meeting.

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

207

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
This resolution seeks to require the Master to report to the Lodge his reasons when he has excluded a brother from a Stated Meeting. The proponents
believe that a Master could use his authority to exclude a member as a way to
sway a ballot or vote.
At present, if the Master wishes to exclude a brother, all he needs to do is
inform the brother that he is not welcome. No further action is required. If
this resolution passes, the Master would be required to inform the brother,
and additionally, report his reasons to the Lodge for the Secretary to include
in the minutes of the meeting.
The proposed change would provide a permanent record for review and
perhaps add some transparency and more disclosure than what currently
exists. It is possible that such transparency could cause some Masters to think
twice before using their power. Additionally, having a written record would
give a brother the opportunity to refute the Master’s reason if he believed that
the Master excluded him for erroneous reasons.
However, for Masters who have refused admission or excluded a brother
for legitimate reasons, he now has to report to the Lodge and create a permanent record of that brother’s transgressions. For instance, if a brother
was refused admission because he was intoxicated, rather than being able to
handle it quietly and whisper good council, the Master would be required to
tell everyone in that meeting and because it would be included in the minutes,
it would be read at the subsequent Stated Meeting as well.
While there could be some benefits from having this requirement in place,
it is unclear whether the passage of this resolution would address the proponents’ stated concerns. This is because a Master who is willing to exclude
brothers for improper reasons is not likely to volunteer those improper reasons for the minutes, but is more likely to fabricate the justification.
Resolution: FAILED

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 807.020 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§807.020. ADDITIONAL REGULATIONS APPLICABLE TO MEETINGS.
A. Sunday Meetings. No stated or special meetings of a lodge shall
be held on Sunday except for the annual Installation of Officers
or funeral services. If the stated meeting of a lunar lodge falls on a
Sunday, the stated meeting shall be held on the following day.
B. Work to be Done in Lodge of Entered Apprentice Masons. All
business, except examinations in the Candidate’s Lecture of the
Fellow Craft and Master Mason degrees, the conferring of the Fellow
Craft and Master Mason degrees, and the consideration of relief

Craft and Master Mason degrees.
C. Quorum. A lodge shall not be opened, nor shall any work be done

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

or business transacted, except by, or in the presence of, and under
the continual direction of the Master, the ranking Warden, the Grand
Master or the Grand Master’s designated representative. No lodge
shall transact any business with fewer than five members of the lodge
present except the conferring of degrees. The Tiler is present while
he is at his post in the Tiler’s room.
D. Presence of Charter. No meeting shall be conducted by a lodge
unless the charter of the lodge (or, in the case of a lodge under dispensation, the dispensation) is present. A photocopy of the charter

The Pledge of Allegiance repeated at all meetings of a lodge. At the
annual election of officers, and at such other meetings as may be
deemed desirable by the Master, the Flag shall be formally presented
at the Altar and received in the manner prescribed in the Ritual. The
Altar of a lodge shall not be decorated with any flag.
F. No Smoking. Smoking (including the use of electronic smoking
devices) is forbidden in the lodge room at all times when the lodge is
in session.
G. No Adjourned Meetings. There shall be no adjourned meeting.
Each meeting of a lodge must be closed when the business proposed
for transaction has been concluded, but in no event later than the
close of the day on which it was opened.
H. Good Standing Requirement. No member may make a motion,
second a motion, speak on a motion, vote on a motion, recommend
anyone for membership or ballot on membership at a lodge meeting
unless he is then a member in good standing of that lodge. He must
present a current dues receipt to the Tiler to demonstrate that he is
a member of the lodge in good standing or be verified by the Master,
Senior Warden, Junior Warden, Secretary or Assistant Secretary as a
member of the lodge in good standing. If a member is present who is
not in good standing, any question or action to be decided hereunder
by a majority or greater vote of the members present shall be decided
by a majority or greater vote of the members present who are in good
standing.

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The proponents of this resolution seek to require the Pledge of Allegiance
at every Masonic meeting. Accordingly, this resolution would amend California
Masonic Code, section 807.020 to require the Pledge of Allegiance be repeated
at all meetings of a lodge. This would include all Stated Meetings and Special
Meetings, which essentially means any meeting where minutes are required.
Currently, Lodges are only required to repeat the Pledge of Allegiance
during Stated Meetings in November, when the Flag is required to be escorted.
Protecting Lodge autonomy has been important to this Grand Lodge
since its formation. Some practices are beneficial for some Lodges, and not
others. Mandating practices has typically arisen from legal requirements or a
compelling reason.
The question before this Grand Lodge is whether Lodges should be
required to repeat the Pledge of Allegiance at every Stated Meeting and
Special Meeting or whether Lodges should retain their current discretion on
the matter.
Resolution: FAILED

Resolution No. 19-07:
Permits Lodges To Meet No Fewer
Than Four Times Annually
The proponents of this resolution seek to permit a lodge to meet no fewer
than four times annually.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the California Masonic Code requires lodges to hold a stated
meeting in each calendar month, with exceptions provided for lunar lodges,
and specific named lodges to meet only ten times a year; and
WHEREAS, across the United Grand Lodge of England, and in many grand
lodges in the United States, lodges have the choice to determine the meeting
schedule that works best for that lodge, be that weekly, twice a month, twelve
times a year, or four times a year, and Masonry thrives in all combinations of
those meeting schedules; and
WHEREAS, the autonomy of the California Masonic Lodge is well established.
lodges may choose their name, meeting place, dues, fees, whom to elect and
when to meet. An extension of choosing how often to meet is a natural extension of the authority granted to California Masonic lodges to govern their own
affairs as they can do best; and
WHEREAS, California Masonic lodges are best poised to make decisions for
themselves and govern themselves; and
WHEREAS, should a lodge elect to meet quarterly, this would not prevent
additional gatherings for practicing ritual and floor-work proficiency to
develop degree conferral ability, the installation of officers, and other education or social activities.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 807.000 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:

212

Proceedings of the

§807.000. STATED MEETINGS.
A lodge shall hold a stated meeting for the transaction of business
once in each calendar month at least once quarterly, on the date
(other than a Sunday) and at the time established in its bylaws. The
foregoing notwithstanding, lodges whose bylaws provide for monthly
meetings fixed by the phase of the moon shall hold a stated meeting for the transaction of business once in each lunar month, and
Mountain Range Lodge No. 18, Harmony Lodge No. 164, Truckee
Lodge No. 200, Big Bear Lodge No. 617 and Rim of the World Lodge
No. 711 shall only be required to hold a stated meeting for the transaction of business once in each of 10 calendar months during the
year, as it may provide in its bylaws.
A lodge may be opened for a stated meeting prior to the time fixed
in its bylaws. However, no business shall be transacted prior to such
time.
The Inspector or Grand Master may grant a dispensation to change
the date of a stated meeting, as provided Section 405.060 of this
code.
In the event that the Master of a lodge determines that inclement
weather, including but not limited to ice, snow, and flood conditions,
or non-weather related unsafe conditions, including but not limited
to flood, fire, earthquake, civil disturbance and the like, existing on
the day established in the bylaws of the lodge for its stated meeting,
makes it hazardous for members of the lodge to attend the meeting,
he may, with the concurrence and consent of the Inspector of the
district to which the Lodge is assigned, postpone the stated meeting
to the same day of the week next following the week scheduled for
the stated meeting. The Master shall notify, to the extent possible, all
members of the lodge residing within fifty miles of the meeting place
of the lodge of the date of the postponed stated meeting.
Should a stated meeting be postponed, the business transacted at
the postponed stated meeting shall be limited to the reading of the
minutes of the last stated and subsequent special meetings, action
thereon, payment of the invoices of the lodge, and such other business of an important nature as determined by the Master to require
immediate consideration. No other new business shall be considered.

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The proponents of this Resolution seek to amend the California Masonic
Code, sections 802.020 and 807.000 to allow a Lodge to amend its by-laws to
hold Stated Meetings as few as four times a year.
The proponents state that other jurisdictions, including the United Grand
Lodge of England and some in the United States, have less than monthly meetings and that system works well for them. They also feel individual Lodges
should have as much flexibility as possible.
CMC, sections 805.220 and 805.230 require a Lodge to receive annual
reports from the Treasurer and Secretary in February and semi-annual reports
in August. Sections 805.410 and 809.510 also require a Lodge to hold the election of officers in November and to adopt a budget no later than January. While
a budget could be adopted prior to January, perhaps in November, the requirement of the reports from the Secretary and Treasurer and election of officers
would require meetings in February, August, and November. Depending upon
the number of bills to be paid some Lodges may not be able to meet fewer than
12 times annually, thereby creating inconsistencies in the Jurisdiction.
If adopted, this proposal would have the potential to tempt struggling
Lodges to reduce the number of their meetings for convenience, and that
could be problematic for some of them. There is value in having monthly
Stated Meetings, as it helps reinforce friendships and encourages good fellowship. A struggling Lodge would be authorized to reduce the number of its
Stated Meetings, and that could create additional difficulties.
On the other hand, this proposal may be beneficial for some Lodges. Some
rural Lodges have limited memberships and have difficulty meeting monthly.
Other Lodges may not have a business need to meet monthly and may want to
repurpose meeting nights.
Adoption of this proposal would be a significant change to the CMC and
how Lodges operate in California. If adopted, this resolution has the potential
to be beneficial to some Lodges and detrimental to others.
Resolution: CARRYOVER

Resolution No. 19-08:
Permits Partial Remission of Dues
The proponents of this resolution seek to permit the partial remission of
dues and reduce a lodge’s per capita contributions prorata based on such partial remissions.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the Charity Committee has the power to recommend the remission of dues of a member; and
WHEREAS, there is a dignity in meeting our obligations, including the payment of dues; and
WHEREAS, should a member be unable to pay his dues, but would like to
pay what he is able to afford, currently there is no mechanism to respect his
wishes; and
WHEREAS, every lodge’s dues are different, and personal situations vary
greatly. The Charity Committee should be permitted to determine the amount
of the remission and judge each case using the same criteria it uses now to
determine if a member deserves charity.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 809.360 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§809.360. REMISSION OF DUES.
If recommended by the Charity Committee, a lodge, without giving
the name of the delinquent Masons except to the Secretary, may
remit to December 31st of the current calendar year the accrued
dues, or a portion thereof, of those of its Masons who are unable to
pay.
The Charity Committee should review the situation of a Mason
whose dues were remitted by a lodge the preceding calendar year
before the February stated meeting. If, in the opinion of the Charity

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

217

Committee, the necessity for the remission of his dues still exists, it
shall recommend to the lodge that the dues be remitted to December
31st of the current calendar year. A lodge shall not remit the dues
of any of its Masons, for any stated period, or in advance, except as
herein provided.
A Mason who is mentally incompetent to such an extent as to be
incapable of taking care of himself, or a member who is a resident
of the Masonic Homes of California, may be considered as unable to
pay dues.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 407.025 of the California Masonic
Code be amended as marked:
§407.025. PER CAPITA LODGE CONTRIBUTIONS.
Each lodge, whether chartered or under dispensation:
A. Shall pay with its Annual Returns the following contributions:
1. For each Mason carried on its rolls as of June 30th, such per
capita sum, not less than $.50, as Grand lodge requires, except
as provided in paragraph A.2 below;
2. For each Mason carried on its rolls as of June 30th whose
dues were partially remitted pursuant to Section 809.360 of
this code, a percentage of the per capita sum otherwise due
under this code equal to the percentage of lodge dues payable
by such Mason for the applicable year;
23.

Each Mason carried on its rolls as of June 30th, such per
capita sum as Grand Lodge levies for the support of Masonic
Homes of California; and

34.

Each Mason carried on its rolls as of June 30th, the per capita
sum of $1.00 for the support of George Washington Masonic
National Memorial;

B. Shall not pay per capita sums for:
1. Masons whose dues have been fully remitted by lodge action
for the preceding calendar year, and
2. Masons whose dues have been remitted because of residence in the Masonic Homes of California.

218

Proceedings of the

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
California Masonic Code, section 809.360 currently allows a Lodge to
remit the dues of a brother who is unable to pay their dues for the current
calendar year. Proponents of this legislation seek to allow a Lodge to remit a
portion of dues owed by a brother, allowing a brother to pay what he is able
towards his dues for the year.
Proponents assert that brothers take pride in paying their dues, and for
some, being unable to pay for a given year lowers their sense of dignity. A
brother facing hardship may feel less embarrassed if he could pay at least some
of his dues.
This resolution would also benefit Lodges financially because a Lodge
would receive some dues from its members that would otherwise be forfeited
if remitted in whole. The Lodge would be charged per capita only on the percentage of dues it receives from the brother.
While this resolution would result in some brothers who are in need
paying less than others during a given year, the partial remission of dues would
remain anonymous through the Lodge’s charity committee.
Report from the Finance Committee:
Resolution 19-08 permits the partial remission of dues and reduces a
Lodge’s per capita contributions prorate based on such partial remission.
To the extent that a Lodge remits the partial dues of a brother it otherwise
would not have remitted at all, the Grand Lodge budget will be negatively
impacted by the reduced per capita contribution. To the extent that a Lodge
partially remits the dues of a brother it otherwise would have remitted the
entire amount thereof, the Grand Lodge budget improves by the increased
contribution. We cannot accurately project Lodge dues remission decisions.
This Resolution, if adopted, will likely have a minimal impact on the Grand
Lodge budget one way or the other.
Resolution: CARRYOVER

Resolution No. 19-09:
Requires Application for Reimbursement
of Mileage to Grand Lodge
The proponents of this resolution seek to require an application for reimbursement for mileage to the Annual Communication.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Grand Lodge “shall pay” the cost of round-trip transportation;
and
WHEREAS, such “round-trip transportation” is not defined property and
does not do justice to current modes of transportation and associated costs;
and
WHEREAS, Grand Lodge reimburses mileage from the lodge location to
Grand Lodge based upon current mileage rates whether or not a lodge needs
or requests such reimbursement.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 407.065 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§407.065. REIMBURSEMENT OF LODGE OFFICERS AND
REPRESENTATIVES.
At the close of each Annual Communication, Grand Lodge shall pay to
the officers or the representatives of each Constituent Lodge present,
the cost of round trip transportation for one person from the location
of the lodge to the place of the Communication, at the rate fixed by the
Committee on Finance, provided that:
1. The lodge has paid its dues to Grand Lodge in full; and
2. An officer or representative has been in attendance at the
Communication from the first day through the last day, unless
excused by Grand Lodge; and

220

Proceedings of the

An application for such reimbursement on a form provided by the
Grand Secretary shall have been filed no later than 30 days after the
close of such Annual Communication.
C. The mileage used for such payment calculations shall be determined
from published records of the California State Automobile Association.
Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The proponents of this resolution seek to modify California Masonic
Code, section 407.065 by clarifying the process of reimbursements authorized
under this section.
Currently, after the close of each Annual Communication, the Grand
Lodge automatically reimburses certain travel expenses to each constituent
Lodge in attendance, provided they have paid their dues. If adopted, this resolution would only require reimbursement if the Lodge requests it.
It should be noted that the reimbursement benefit for each Constituent
Lodge that qualify would not been altered or changed in any manner. But a
form would need be submitted on or before 30 days following the conclusion
of such Annual Communication to facilitate reimbursement.
It is a standard and accepted practice of business entities across all disciplines to require proper verifiable expenses before the accounting department
will issue a reimbursement check. The manner of verification may require
itemized expenses or a signed affidavit attesting to the expense s before
a check is issued. This resolution will assist our Grand Lodge Accounting
Department to resolve any potential legal issues that may arise, as well, as the
expeditious processing, balancing and reconciliation of expenses associated
with Section 407.065.
Report from the Finance Committee:
Resolution 19-09 requires a Lodge to submit an application for reimbursement of mileage to the Annual Communication. To the extent that a
Lodge (or Lodges) does not apply for reimbursement when it is otherwise
entitled to, the Grand Lodge budget improves slightly by the eligible amount
not requested. We cannot accurately project the number Lodges that will not
apply for reimbursement even if the lodges are so entitled. The average lodge
reimbursement is $60.00. This Resolution, if adopted, will likely have a very
minimal impact on the Grand Lodge budget.
Resolution: CARRYOVER

REPORT OF THE
BOARD OF TRUSTEES
MASONIC HOMES OF CALIFORNIA

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & A.M. of California:
I am proud to share that over the past year, our Masonic Homes served
more than 1,250 Bbrothers and their wives, widows, and families—including more than 750 on our campuses and more than 500 clients through
our Masonic Center for Youth and Families (MCYAF). Through Masonic
Outreach Services (MOS), another 450 Masonic family members received
support in their communities, close to their lodges and families.
More than 300 Masons, wives, and widows are thriving our Union City
and Covina campuses. Five residents are in our 100+ club, and our eldest resident celebrated her 106th birthday this month. In addition to high-quality
independent and assisted living care, our skilled nursing program in Union
City serves Masons and their families who require more advanced nursing
home care. For many families, knowing that their loved ones will be cared for
at the Masonic Home has been a godsend.
This important, life-changing service is soon coming to Covina, where we
have long needed a skilled nursing and memory care facility. Now, thanks to
your generosity through the Let’s Write the Future campaign, we are able to
make that dream a reality. Partners will no longer need to be separated in
what may be their darkest hour. Our new, 32-bed skilled nursing center, which
will offer memory and long-term care, is currently under construction on the
Covina campus and will be open in 2020. And that can’t come soon enough—
our waiting list has grown to 26, split evenly between memory care and longterm care. This state-of-the-art facility will improve the quality of life for our
members in sSouthern California and help fulfill our obligation to always care
for our fraternal family members in need.
Memory care continues to remain a primary focus at the Masonic Homes,
as Alzheimer’s disease and dementia statistics rise each year. Our innovative

224

Proceedings of the

memory care program, Stepping Stones, provides strategies to address the
progression of memory loss and continues to yield positive outcomes. The
Brain Gym helps residents sharpen their memory through neurologist-designed computer stimulation, and through the Compass Club memory care
program, we have continued to demonstrate that memory loss progression
can be slowed—and in some cases even reversed.
We are also serving more of our fraternal family than ever with our
Masonic Outreach Services programs. In addition to a higher volume of
information and referral calls, the MOS staff made more than 1,000 home
visits over the past year to help ensure our fraternal family is safe. Many of
these brothers, wives, and widows required financial assistance in order to
afford even basic necessities and housing. As need continues to expand in
the Central Valley, so do our services in this area, as well as in other underserved areas.
The important Lodge Outreach Program, which trains volunteer Masons
to lead outreach efforts locally, extends MOS’s reach while meaningfully
engaging members and reconnecting absent brothers with their lodges.
This year also saw two new move-ins to our shared housing program on
the Covina campus, which offers safe, affordable housing to independent
seniors. This innovative approach utilizes the former children’s homes and
offers the benefits of living independently but in a community of like-minded
people.
The Masonic Value Network, which helps members conveniently and
independently research and access care in their own communities, continues
to grow as well. The prescription discount service is an especially popular service for our membership. This year we’ve added new retirement communities
to the network.
And through our Masonic Center for Youth and Families programs, we’ve
begun to reach more Masons and their families than ever before. Last year, we
expanded MCYAF to Covina, and this year, we’ve begun to provide high-quality mental health services to members when they find themselves in need, and
to lodges when they find themselves in crisis.
In addition, a pilot program, complete with staff training across both campuses and MOS staff, began to provide elderly residents with mental health
services. Often, undiagnosed depression leads to memory loss and, worse, a
feeling of hopelessness for the elderly. In fact, suicide rates among the elderly
far exceed those of teens and young adults? This new and important service
offered by the Masonic Center for Youth and Families will seek to address this
frequently unrecognized need.
But that doesn’t mean that our dedication to youth and families has
diminished. We reached more than 1,200 people through community

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

225

outreach and presentations, launched an anti-bullying program for the
Masonic youth orders. In Covina, MCYAF has built a reputation with the
Child Advocacy Center, Service Area Advisory Committee 3, comprised of
leaders in the fields of social services and mental health in Los Angeles,
and with the Covina Police Department, all of whom hold our services in
the highest esteem. In tandem with its San Francisco center, MCYAF continues to grow its service area through the telehealth counseling program
to reach even more Masonic families statewide.
Our campus master plan in Union City continues to evolve in the wake of
our breaking ground on a new state-of-the-art memory care and assisted living
center. We also began renovations on two 60-year-old buildings to increase
capacity. We are improving our facilities to provide more outdoor space and
activities for residents to enjoy. Again, thanks to the generosity of our membership, all of these needed renovations will allow us to uphold our obligation
to you, our brothers, that the Masonic Homes will be here when you or your
loved ones need us.
Our broader community is also important to us. To celebrate, we have
held events year-round that bring our neighbors onto our campuses. This
year was no exception: The holiday tree lighting in Union City, which is a tradition for hundreds of our neighbors; our first ever tree-lighting in Covina;
an annual chili cook-off honoring police and firemen; and the Luminary
Caregiver Awards, which recognize the contributions of the people who
make a difference in the lives of those suffering from Alzheimer’s disease
and dementia. SummerFest and HarvestFest, which will pivot campuses
next year, brings thousands of Masons to the Homes. And this fall, we will
begin a new tradition with our partnership with the Alzheimer’s Walk in
the East Bay, to help finally find a cure for this devastating disease. We
hope you will walk with us.
All of this can’t be done without an energized staff, and I’m proud to
share that the Masonic Homes has been named one of the Top Workplaces in
2019 by the Bay Area News Group. Drawing on survey results measuring factors like company values and employee connection to its mission, the entire
Masonic Homes staff deserves the accolades for making the Masonic Homes
of California a great place to work and live. We are incredibly proud of this
recognition. Our work with the Masonic Homes Way has helped revitalize our
culture and commitment to our members, residents, and clients.
For more than 100 years, the Masonic Homes of California has provided
relief to brothers and their wives, widows, and children in need. Our commitment to our obligation is stronger today than ever. The Masonic Home will be
here when you need us, and as always, we are committed to serving you now
and in the future.

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS
Acacia Creek Retirement Community

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
Acacia Creek, our continuing care retirement community, is now in its ninth
year of operation. Financially, Acacia Creek continues to meet its 25-year pro
forma and, each year, meets its annual payment on bonds. Fiscal year 2019 has
proven to be the strongest in Acacia Creek’s history due to increased revenue
and aggressive expense controls. As a result, Acacia Creek is positioned well
for the 2020 fiscal year.
I am pleased to share that Acacia Creek’s average occupancy of 96 percent remains well above the national average of 89 percent for occupancy in
independent continuing care retirement communities. Our marketing program is focused on expanding our active wait list and reselling apartments as
soon as we are aware of a projected transition. Acacia Creek has benefitted
from resident transitions which have tracked with the 2019 budget, allowing
the community to project a year-end occupancy rate in the mid- to high 90th
percentile.
Acacia Creek’s success is driven by its current residents’ satisfaction and
happiness, which infuses the campus with vitality. These important qualities
were evaluated in this year’s resident survey, which indicated resident satisfaction at an astounding 96.5 percent. Residents’ joyful spirit is apparent to
prospective buyers and visitors, whether they are joining us for a meal, touring
the campus, or staying overnight in one of our well-appointed guest suites.
Acacia Creek residents demonstrate—through collected data—that they enjoy
better health, nutrition, and physical activity than those at comparable communities elsewhere in the country.
Thanks to this data and other intensive documentation, Acacia Creek has
been recognized as a certified Center for Successful Aging since 2016. One of just
19 communities nationwide, and the only one in Northern California, this designation positions Acacia Creek as a flagship community for Successful Aging, a
concept inspired by the MacArthur Foundation’s 10-year study on aging.
This certification is awarded to communities that have provided intensive
documentation, over five years, of a culture in which residents can continue to
grow and thrive. This has been achieved through the leadership’s commitment

246

Proceedings of the

to continually assessing and implementing policies and procedures in order to
meet the ever-changing needs of our residents. We do this by providing opportunities in advanced programming involving the physical, spiritual, social, and
intellectual growth of our residents as the anchor of our Successful Aging
Philosophy. Over the past year, the leadership team successfully completed
the rigorous documentation to successfully validate a three-year re-certification as a Center for Successful Aging.
Our partnership with Masterpiece Living, a national organization which
provides Acacia Creek with education and programs of physical and mental
wellness, is an important part of the residents’ success. Through Masterpiece
Living programs, Acacia Creek residents are empowered to pursue new skills,
physical activities, and personal fulfillment, as well as contribute to the Acacia
Creek community. This year (2019), the leadership team has focused on training and educating all team members and their families in successful aging to
encourage healthy living. This includes opportunities for continuing education through our scholarship program.
Acacia Creek has influence in its greater community as well. Residents
have been espousing these successful aging concepts by sharing their skills,
knowledge, social activity, and life experiences away from the campus. Some
examples of our interaction within the greater community are volunteering
with the local grade schools, high schools, senior centers, community soup
kitchens, and performing outreach presentations to senior groups and business groups on successful aging.
Acacia Creek continues to benefit from the camaraderie between Masonic
and non-Masonic residents. Thirteen residents and staff members have
already joined the fraternity, including administrator Martin Herter. We hope
that many more will decide to petition in the years to come. Acacia Creek
Masons are active in Siminoff Daylight Lodge at the Masonic Home.
Acacia Creek team members, who follow a team management concept,
report a positive work environment which is reflected in low turnover. Team
members are decision makers who feel a sense of ownership in the community’s operations and play a vital role in making the community an ideal place to
live. Staffing has been stable at Acacia Creek for the past two years. The annual
turnover rate of 23 percent is significantly lower than the industry average of
33 percent. Additionally, there has been no turnover in the leadership team in
more than three years.
The fraternity envisioned that Acacia Creek would include all levels
of health care, from independent and assisted living to skilled nursing and
memory care. The Masonic Homes and Acacia Creek boards continue to collaborate to expand and improve services on both campuses. The Acacia Creek
community, together with the boards of the Masonic Homes and Acacia Creek,
is working to further improve the lives of current residents with new offerings.
For instance, as part of its Campus Master Plan, this year the Masonic Homes
began construction on Acacia Creek’s new Memory Support and Assisted

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

247

Living building across the street from the existing building. Completion is
expected in 2021. This project will ensure increased capacity and services for
the residents of Acacia Creek.
The board wishes to extend its sincere appreciation to Chuck Major, president of Acacia Creek, and Martin Herter, vice president and administrator,
who have maintained the high level of morale and accountability of the staff,
for executing the strategic marketing plan that has maintained Acacia Creek’s
occupancy stabilization and for ensuring the high-quality lifestyle for our residents that is the vision and goal of Acacia Creek.
I want to thank the members of the Grand Lodge Executive Committee,
Grand Lodge staff, the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees, and the Acacia
Creek Board of Directors for their expertise, their vision, and their passion.
We are excited about our future, and together we look forward to ensuring the
continued success and support of the mission of Acacia Creek.
Respectfully submitted,
Kenneth G. Nagel, PGM, Chairman
Charles W. Major, President
Martin Herter, Vice President
