REPORT OF THE BOARD OF TRUSTEES
California Masonic Foundation

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
Building upon last year’s success as the fundraising arm of the Fraternity,
the California Masonic Foundation has exceeded all expectations in 2019 and
helped the Grand Lodge of California achieve far more than it originally anticipated. Our Let’s Write the Future campaign, led by Chairman R. Stephen Doan,
PGM, has inspired lodges up and down the state to connect the dots between
Masonic ritual and the Grand Lodge’s charities, underscoring a message we all
believed we already understood: California Masons live their Masonic values
and give their talents, love, and commitment to all that they value.
The foundation is now concluding the second year of Most Worshipful
Doan’s three-year Let’s Write the Future campaign. The first such campaign in
our jurisdiction in more than 60 years, the campaign set an original fundraising goal of $5 million to fund the expansion of services offered at the Masonic
Homes of California to include skilled nursing and memory care. I’m happy to
report that the campaign has already surpassed our greatest expectations. By
the time our second year has concluded, lodge and individual donations will
exceed $7 million—$2 million above our goal. The exceptional generosity of
our Brethren has provided Grand Lodge leadership with the necessary funding
to imagine even better things for the future.
But that isn’t the only success the foundation has enjoyed over the past
year. To be most effective, the foundation interacts with each of our boards
and provides leadership in the advancement of current and future initiatives.
Previous fundraising commitments were aimed at developing a new generation
of Masonic leadership. Today, Masters, Wardens, Secretaries, and Treasurers
of constituent lodges are able to attend retreats, which are dedicated to providing leadership lessons that we hope will radiate out into the wider world.
Other foundation commitments to public schools and children can be seen
in our partnership with the Raising-A-Reader children’s literacy program and
Masons4Mitts, which now works with four of the five Major League Baseball
teams in the state.
Among our other successes, the foundation supported the UCLA Academic
Symposium, which hosted many of the world’s top Masonic academics.

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

249

Furthermore, the foundation’s Investment in Success program continues to
support promising young men and women pursuing a college education, and
our scholarship funding also reaches Masonic youth leaders, as originally established by M.W.M. David Perry, to assist with the costs of a college education.
The foundation’s statewide Public Schools Advisory Councils continued
their great work this year. These dedicated Brethren visited lodges and raised
funds for childhood literacy, worked with school districts to plan and execute our Public Schools Month kickoff events in April, and interviewed and
selected recipients for the Investment in Success scholarship. This year, they,
along with our Grand Master, helped present more than $739,000 to support
literacy and college success at these kickoff events. The participation by members at these celebrations, the increased number of students in our scholarship program, and the expanded number of classrooms implementing RaisingA-Reader are testimony to their success. I thank the chairman and all of the
members of each Advisory Council for making a profound difference in the
lives of California students.
Our partnership with Raising-A-Reader continues to produce results—the
name has become the brand by which California Masons identify the fulfillment of their commitment to public schools. The familiar bags and books have
now made their way into nearly 700 classrooms, giving the gift of knowledge
and the keys to success to hundreds of young children who might otherwise
have been denied access to these resources. Looking ahead, Raising-A-Reader
will soon reach more than 1,000 California public school classrooms.
For the 25th consecutive year, California Masons supported the California
Teacher of the Year program. As a major and one of the longest-running contributors, the California Masonic Foundation and Grand Lodge of California
were honored by the state Superintendent of Schools at the annual awards
gala in Sacramento. It was my pleasure to join foundation president Doug
Ismail to deliver our checks of gratitude to the heroes of the classroom.
Our Masons4Mitts program, in its 11th year, also continued to strike a
chord with Masons. Captains and their teams raised more than $170,000 to
purchase mitts for youth through the foundations of the San Francisco Giants,
Los Angeles Dodgers, San Diego Padres, and the Los Angeles Angels. Many
Brethren attended the games in all four cities and watched as our Grand
Master made check presentations on the field. Our total contributions to this
program over the past 10 years exceed $1 million.
The trustees thank Most Worshipful Wright for the opportunity to serve.
We also wish to thank our board president, Brother Doug Ismail, along with
Candler Gibson, Greg Cherry, Denise Avila, Josh Castro, and Julia Gordon for
their tireless efforts. Your dedication and commitment to the board and its
charitable mission are always above and beyond the call of duty.
The board of trustees is extremely pleased with the culture of philanthropy demonstrated by California Masons. We now look forward to continuing our campaign and look forward to the years ahead. The Fraternity’s 2020

250

Proceedings of the

Strategic Plan ends on Oct. 31, 2020. A new 2025 Strategic Plan will take its
place. Before it does, it must be planned, organized, staffed, and implemented.
The California Masonic Foundation is already doing its part by leaning into all
that our charities are doing so that our future fundraising is matched with our
goals and expectations.
Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF TRUSTEES
California Masonic Memorial Temple
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
The California Masonic Memorial Temple (CMMT) is proud to report
another successful year and the completion of a significant milestone in the
history of the building.
Overall, CMMT operations have again been strong, and Live Nation
remains a solid tenant and partner, continuing to present high-quality concerts and corporate events. Financial performance remains strong and predictable. Positive cash flow for the year is forecasted at more than $500,000,
continuing the steady year-over-year increase we have seen the past several
years. In all, more than 200,000 people visited the Memorial Temple this year
to attend concerts, private events, or take a tour.
In 2018, the CMMT contracted a professional firm to undertake a survey
of the building and its systems. The study did not reveal any significant issues
and confirmed the generally good condition of the 61-year old structure. The
study did, however, identify a number of systems that will need to be repaired
or replaced over the next decade. This summer, the CMMT Board of Directors
approved a 10-year capital plan to address the needs outlined in the report,
including improvements to the elevators, HVAC, plumbing, mechanical systems, power sources, safety equipment, and the exterior building envelope.
According to the plan, all improvements will be paid for through operating
cash flow. The board established a new building improvement reserve fund
for these purposes.
Our relationship with our neighbors remains close, as CMMT holds quarterly meetings through the Nob Hill Community Liaison Group. Executive
Vice President and Secretary Allan Casalou continues to serve as a director
of the Nob Hill Association and on the Huntington Park Committee, chaired
by our own Khalil Sweidy, a Nob Hill resident. CMMT supports the annual
Huntington Park tree lighting ceremony, which attracts hundreds of spectators to Nob Hill each year.
That said, the most exciting development at CMMT in decades has
been the completion of Freemasons’ Hall, the first lodge hall to be built in
the CMMT. Designed to suit the needs of a smaller, more connected modern
lodge, Freemasons’ Hall incorporates traditional Masonic symbolism but

252

Proceedings of the

also integrates symbolism from the ritual never seen in lodge rooms before.
It draws on sacred geometry and ancient architecture in many of its design
features. In addition to addressing the growing demand for lodge meeting
spaces in downtown San Francisco, the new hall provides a beautiful facility for Masons and guests from around the world to visit, and for lodges to
meet and practice the Craft. In September alone, there were 21 lodge events in
Freemasons’ Hall. The CMMT invites all California lodges to consider using
Freemasons’ Hall for special meetings and degrees.
We hope that members will make a point of visiting CMMT and
Freemasons’ Hall whenever they’re in San Francisco, and also see the unique
collections in the Henry Wilson Coil Library and Museum and the remarkable
endomosaic mural in our lobby, designed and constructed by Emile Norman.
The board wishes to extend its appreciation to our executive vice president, Grand Secretary Allan Casalou; our chief financial officer, Thomas J.
Boyer; our director of financial planning and real estate, Khalil Sweidy; our
general counsel, Andy Cameron; and Grand Treasurer Arthur Salazar. We
would also like to thank Julia Gordon for her work in preparing and managing
our board meetings and materials, as well as Joe Evans for his excellent curation and management of the Henry Wilson Coil Library and Museum collections. Our sincere thanks and appreciation also go out to the staff who work
so diligently in representing our interests and maintaining and managing the
building. Finally, we thank our Grand Master, Most Worshipful Stuart Wright,
for the opportunity to serve and for his active support of our efforts.
Respectfully submitted,
William J. Bray III, PGM, Chairman and President
Allan L. Casalou, Executive Vice President and Secretary

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF TRUSTEES
Nob Hill Masonic Center
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
The Board of Trustees for the Nob Hill Masonic Center (NHMC) is pleased
to present this annual report to the Grand Lodge of California and its members. As the Grand Lodge’s only for-profit entity, our primary goal is ensuring the efficient and effective operation of the California Masonic Memorial
Temple garage in order to generate an annual dividend for the Grand Lodge of
California, its sole stockholder.
This year, the NHMC parking operation maintained strong revenue and
has continued to evolve into a mobility hub in the heart of San Francisco. First
and foremost, NHMC was again able to provide the required dividend payment to the Grand Lodge of California in the amount of $395,000. Profits for
this current fiscal year are expected to be approximately $490,000, which will
fund the next dividend and create reserves for future dividends.
We’ve achieved this through a diverse revenue portfolio including daily,
monthly, and event parking; hotel and restaurant valet parking; car-share
parking; and electric vehicle charging stations. We continue to benefit from
our recent, well-planned infrastructure changes, including garage automation
and solar energy. The 2017 solar energy installation has been a benefit to our
bottom line, with at least an 80 percent reduction in energy costs.
To promote occupancy of the garage throughout the day, we continue
our relationship with car-sharing services including ZipCar, Getaround, and
Scoot—a two-wheeled scooter-sharing company. We expanded our current
electric vehicle charging footprint in a new agreement with Tesla, which
resulted in the Spring installation of nine Tesla Level 2 charging stations.
In addition to our building signage and word-of-mouth advertising, NHMC
markets the garage through a number of online channels. Our main online
presence is the parking guide at sfmasonic.parkingguide.com. We continue to
advertise on driving apps such as Waze Navigation, Yext, and Google Maps, as
well as place online ads through Live Nation. Our online digital ads appear on
Google, Bing, Yelp, Foursquare, Facebook, and MapQuest. Such advertising
helps us to raise public awareness of the Masonic garage as a parking option on
Nob Hill and allows riders to reserve a parking space in advance of their visit
to our venue or other destinations on and around Nob Hill.

254

Proceedings of the

In summary, NHMC’s success throughout the past year has been due to
our ability to control costs, grow and diversify revenue, and harness marketing
efforts through the various online digital channels.
As we close out our fiscal year, we would like to thank the Grand Lodge
staff for their hard work managing the operations of the garage. Thank you to
our fellow colleagues on the board of directors for the wisdom and counsel
they have provided throughout the year.
Most Worshipful Wright, it has been an honor for this year’s board to
serve you and this Grand Lodge. We appreciate your support and continue to
pledge to achieve our goal of delivering the very best and highest dividend possible to the Grand Lodge of California. Congratulations to you for a fantastic
year and your leadership and labors on behalf of our Fraternity.
Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON FINANCE

In accordance with California Masonic Code §406.035, the Grand Lodge
Committee on Finance has reviewed the resolutions to be considered at the
170th Annual Communication and has prepared the following estimate of the
cost impact of each to Grand Lodge, if adopted.
Carry-Over Legislation
The committee has reviewed carry-over legislation from 2018 and finds that
none of this legislation will have a financial impact on the Grand Lodge budget.
New Resolutions
The committee has reviewed the new resolutions 19-01 through 19-09 and
finds that none of this legislation will have a financial impact on the Grand
Lodge budget, except for resolutions 19-08 and 19-09.

Resolution 19-08
Permits Partial Remission of Dues
Resolution 19-08 permits the partial remission of dues and reduces a
Lodge’s per capita contributions pro rata based on such partial remission.
To the extent that a lodge remits the partial dues of a Brother it otherwise
would not have remitted at all, the Grand Lodge budget will be negatively
impacted by the reduced per capita contribution. To the extent that a lodge
partially remits the dues of a Brother it otherwise would have remitted the
entire amount thereof, the Grand Lodge budget improves by the increased
contribution. We cannot accurately project lodge dues remission decisions.
This resolution, if adopted, will likely have a minimal impact on the Grand
Lodge budget one way or the other.

258

Proceedings of the

Resolution 19-09
Requires Application
for Reimbursementof Mileage to Grand Lodge
Resolution 19-09 requires a lodge to submit an application for reimbursement of mileage to the Annual Communication. To the extent that
a lodge (or lodges) does not apply for reimbursement when it is otherwise
entitled to, the Grand Lodge budget improves slightly by the eligible amount
not requested. We cannot accurately project the number lodges that will not
apply for reimbursement even if the lodges are so entitled. The average lodge
reimbursement is $60.00. This resolution, if adopted, will likely have a very
minimal impact on the Grand Lodge budget.
Certain legislation may propose changes to the Ritual or the Monitor.
It has been a practice of the Grand Lodge to make the printed changes and
produce new ciphers and Monitors only after the current inventory has been
depleted. Therefore, there is no additional expense for the purpose of reprinting caused by the adoption of such legislation.
Sincerely and fraternally yours,
Levon H. Keshishian, Chairman

REPORT OF THE
COMMITTEE ON INSURANCE

Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
The Masons of California’s corporate insurance program provides the
lodge and hall—as well as the properties of the Masonic Homes, Acacia Creek,
and Nob Hill—with coverage, including property, general liability, umbrella
liability, directors and officers liability, employment and crime insurance policies. These were renewed April 1, 2019.
During this renewal, we were required to accept several changes to the hall
insurance programs for the upcoming year. Each renewal presents challenges.
This year, however, was the most difficult since the great recession of the last
decade. During the last 24 months, insurers have incurred significant losses
due to catastrophic events in California and elsewhere. As a result, insurers
have set higher premium levels and tightened underwriting and policy terms.
Our recent claim histories specifically for the hall exposures have exacerbated
these trends. In the last several years, the hall programs have tended to experience higher claims frequencies, causing insurers to review our programs with
greater underwriting scrutiny.
In response to this challenging environment, we and our insurance
broker, Marsh, reached out to more insurance markets and carriers than in
prior years. However, while insurers’ interest remains significant, their diminished financial conditions—coupled with the complexity of our operations
and claims frequency—limited the constructive responses we received from
potential carriers. Within these limitations, we are confident that we identified the most favorable coverages available to us.

Property Insurance Program Renewal
The renewed Hall, Grand Lodge/MH/AC/MCYF & Acacia Creek Property
Program includes the following key terms and changes from last year:
• Insurer: Lexington (no change from prior year).
• Limits: $200 million.

Conclusions
The increase in deductibles for the property program created a significant
challenge for the organization. Halls and their owners need to develop a plan
to address deferred maintenance that may have accumulated over the years.
Claims related to water damage are the most predominate in our history. The
condition of roofs and window/door caulking are those areas that should be
focused on by the hall. Claims related to poor maintenance may be challenged
by the insurer in the future. This is not a one-year occurrence. Therefore, hall
management should focus on deferred maintenance and starting a preventative
maintenance program.
The casualty program was moved from Liberty Insurance Company to
Travelers Insurance Company at competitive rates. This is a new relationship
and our goal is to try to leverage this into a discussion about the property program in the future.
Overall the program was renewed in what are very difficult and hardening
markets. Insurers are facing huge losses from climate change-related disasters
like fires, hurricanes, and flooding. We see no letup in this trend. Sometimes
these circumstances result in an influx of new money but we have yet to see
that. Overall, we will continue to work with our broker, Marsh, to push underwriters to provide the best terms possible. In addition, we should work with
halls to help them better understand the need to provide realistic replacement cost values and understand good housekeeping and how they relate to
reduced premiums.
Respectfully submitted,
David Forsyth, Chairman
John A. Lindell, Vice Chairman

William M. Zachry

REPORT OF THE
INVESTMENT COMMITTEE

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

Overview
The Investment Committee has been charged with the prudent handling of
Grand Lodge investment funds. These funds consist primarily of the General
and Endowment funds for the Masonic Homes of California, but also include
the investment portfolios of the California Masonic Foundation, California
Masonic Memorial Temple and the Grand Lodge itself.
The financial objectives for these funds we steward are laid out in our
approved Investment Policy Statement:
The primary objectives of the funds are to provide a regular and reliable
source of financial support to the Masonic entity or its beneficiaries, while
preserving the purchasing power of the funds after withdrawals are taken.
In plain English, we are tasked to make sure that the Homes, the
Foundation, and all entities that are entrusting their funds to our care can
expect to receive a reasonable income, while their principle keeps pace with
expected inflation over time.
As a simple example, if one of the entities wanted to be able to rely on a
4.5% distribution from their money, we know we’d have to earn at least that,
by investing. If we also expected inflation to be 2% per year on average (eroding purchasing power of the principal), we’d know that we ALSO want to grow
the principle by 2% per year on average. We’d then know that we needed to
build a portfolio that could reasonably be expected to return 6.5% over the
long-term (4.5% spending + 2% inflation).
This example, while simple, is actually very close to the actual numbers
used to form our return goals for the Grand Lodge investments.
The job of the Committee, then, is to build the portfolio with the best
chance of accomplishing that return goal over the long-term, while exposing
the portfolio to the least risk needed to attain that goal.

264

Proceedings of the

While the committee is comprised of diligent financial professionals who
are astute in portfolio construction and global economics themselves; we also
employ the use of a robust investment consultant team that help us quantify
and evaluate the metrics of our portfolio and model the mix of investments
that give us the greatest likelihood of achieving those goals.
Grand Lodge & Related Entity Investment Performance
for the year ended June 30th, 2019:
The Total Grand Lodge and Related Entities portfolio earned a rate of
return of 5.5% for the year ending June 30, 2019. The total fund policy benchmark was up 6.2%. The market value of the Total Grand Lodge and Related
Entities portfolio as of June 30, 2019, was $989,606,387. For the three-year
period ending June 30, 2019, the combined Grand Lodge and related entities
returned 8.7% versus 8.4% for the benchmark. Since inception, our funds have
returned 7.5% annually versus 7.7% return of the benchmark.

Investment Managers Terminated:
Once managers have been thoroughly vetted and consistently monitored,
as long as the manager’s investment style is still part of our overall investment thesis, it’s relatively rare that a manager gets terminated, unless we
have adjusted the positioning of the portfolio. In the last two years, we have,
indeed, made several positioning changes. Much of the change comes from
our positive effort to create a Private Markets portion of the portfolio.
As part of our fundamental philosophy, stated in our investment policy
statement:
“We believe that manager turnover is very expensive and extremely disruptive to the efficient and productive operation of an investment program.
Managers should be hired with a long-run view… We also believe that constant and/or rapid turnover of managers, justified solely on the basis of relative underperformance is usually an indication of a lack of adherence to the
selection and retention process. In particular, short-term (generally less than
one year) underperformance should not be a reason for termination, unless it
is accompanied by other adverse key retention characteristics.”

Grand Lodge Investment Management
In order to fulfill our responsibilities in accordance with the Grand Lodge
Investment Policy and Philosophy, the Investment Committee meets quarterly with our investment consultant, NEPC, LLC. We also meet with our individual portfolio managers as needed and review due diligence reports quarterly from the consultants. We monitor respective performance of the managers compared to various indices representing their objective. This process
provides the Investment Committee with the necessary data to evaluate each
investment manager on a timely basis, and to observe whether they continue
to achieve the objectives of their mandate.

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

267

The committee also holds ad-hoc conference calls (as needed) to discuss
any outstanding business or discuss the implementation of tactical changes
within the portfolio.
Your Grand Lodge Investment Committee is also available to assist individual lodges in determining appropriate investment strategies. We are also
here to help lodges establish a set of policies and procedures that are designed
to ensure assets are invested according to the needs of the lodge and to safeguard against the misuse of funds. Investment Committee members continue
to make themselves available to the lodges for assistance with this program
and other questions regarding lodge investments.

to ensure that your assets are properly stewarded and I’m glad to have their
efforts and dedication. Thank you for allowing me to serve as chair this year; it
is both an honor and a privilege to work with these gentlemen.
I want to thank Julia Gordon, who tirelessly works to prepare all of our
committees for success, we are immensely blessed by her. I also want to thank
VW Art Salazar, our Grand Treasurer, and Tom Boyer and Linh Pham, who
manage the day to day flows and intricacies of the assets of our related entities. Thank you.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON JURISPRUDENCE

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
The Committee on Jurisprudence serves as the legal adviser to the Grand
Master and the legal adviser to the Grand Lodge when in session. The committee reviews proposed resolutions and recommendations to be considered
at the next Annual Communication and prepares any necessary legislation to
carry out the intent of the proponents. At the Annual Communication, it comments on the legality of the Grand Master’s decisions and dispensations and
on the legal effect of the proposed recommendations and resolutions. After
the Annual Communication, it prepares the changes to the California Masonic
Code to reflect the legislation which was adopted.
In the committee’s view, those of Grand Master Wright’s decisions and
dispensations coming to its attention were legal and within his discretion. In
the committee’s view, the legislation posted by the Grand Secretary to the
Grand Lodge website on August first of this year is sufficient to carry out
the intent of the proponents, and the legislation contained in Grand Master
Wright’s recommendations which he will present in his message is sufficient
to carry out his intent. We believe that each piece of this legislation has the
legal effect set forth in it.
In presenting the legislation for your consideration, we make no recommendations as to the action you should take with it. While the Committee has written
the title and introductory explanation for each resolution before you and assisted
the proponents in drafting the Code changes required to effect their intent, the
proponents’ arguments in their whereas clauses are their own. The committee
does not assist in drafting the whereas clauses and makes no comments on them.
The legislation posted by the Grand Secretary to the Grand Lodge website on August first of this year and the legislation contained in Grand Master
Wright’s recommendations require no separate motion because they are
automatically before this Annual Communication. The presiding officer will
announce the vote required for the passage of each item before discussion
begins. Any legislation which does not amend the California Masonic Code
or the Ritual requires a simple majority only for adoption. Any amendment
to the California Masonic Code or the Ritual must be adopted by a five-sixths

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

275

affirmative vote. If the amendment receives a simple majority but less than a
five-sixths affirmative vote, it carries over to the next Annual Communication
when only a two-thirds affirmative vote is required for adoption.
In addition to the foregoing responsibilities, the committee reviews all
charges and specifications of un-Masonic conduct, strikes out those portions
which are not supported by a clear and precise specification of un-Masonic
conduct and revises those portions which are incorrect, ambiguous or insufficient. The committee may dismiss charges if all the facts set forth in the specifications, even if true, would not warrant a verdict of un-Masonic conduct.
As part of its review, the committee provides the parties with every essential
factual element which must be proven at trial for the accused to be found
guilty of each charge. Since the last Annual Communication, the committee
has reviewed the charges and specifications in 22 trials. We also advised the
Grand Master on charges and specifications filed against a sitting Master.
If a Mason under the disciplinary jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge has
pleaded guilty or nolo contendere (or no contest) to, or has been convicted
of, a crime of moral turpitude by a federal or state court, he shall be deemed
automatically expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry without
any further action of his lodge or Grand Lodge. The committee reviews a certified copy of the record of conviction to determine whether there has been
an automatic expulsion. Since the last Annual Communication, the committee
has reviewed seven federal or state court records to evaluate whether there
has been an automatic expulsion of the Mason involved in the proceeding.
These matters are summarized in the attached exhibit.
No person shall hold or be eligible for membership in any constituent
lodge who has pleaded guilty or nolo contendere to, or has been convicted
of, a crime involving a violation of the moral law unless, for the reason that
he did not commit the offense, he either has been pardoned or had his judgment of conviction vacated or reversed. All applicants are subject to background checks to determine compliance with this rule. Since the last Annual
Communication, the Grand Secretary has asked the committee to review no
federal or state court records to evaluate whether an applicant is eligible for
the degrees.
We thank the Grand Master for the opportunity which he has given us to
serve this year.
Respectfully submitted,
R. Stephen Doan, PGM, Chairman
Michael H. Anatole
David M. Ferreria
Vance T. Langford
Jack R. Levitt, PGM

Automatic Expulsions
October 19, 2018 to October 18, 2019

Trial No. 2667
In Trial No. 2667, the member was convicted of two violations of
California Penal Code Section 487. Under Section 100.075 of the California
Masonic Code and 2009 Grand Master’s Decision No. 2, theft involves moral
turpitude. In the committee’s opinion, the conduct described in California
Penal Code Section 487 involves theft. Therefore, based on the court record
and the foregoing analysis, it is the judgment of a majority of the members
of the Committee on Jurisprudence that the member has been convicted of
a crime of moral turpitude before a state court. Accordingly, the member has
been automatically expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry pursuant to Section 1404.820 of the California Masonic Code. His expulsion from
Masonry was effective on September 29, 2014, the date of his conviction.
Trial No. 2842
In Trial No. 2842, the member pled no contest to two violations of
California Penal Code Section 211. Under Section 100.075 of the California
Masonic Code and 2009 Grand Master’s Decision No. 2, robbery involves
moral turpitude. In the committee’s opinion, the conduct described in
California Penal Code Section 211 involves robbery. Therefore, based on the
Court Record and the foregoing analysis, it is the judgment of a majority of
the members of the Committee on Jurisprudence that the member pled no
contest to a crime of moral turpitude before a state court. Accordingly, the
member has been automatically expelled from all the rights and privileges of
Masonry pursuant to Section 1404.820 of the California Masonic Code. His
expulsion from Masonry was effective on May 24, 2017, the date he entered his
plea of nolo contendere (or no contest).

functions involves moral turpitude. In the committee’s opinion, the conduct
described in 26 U.S.C. §§ 7206(1);(2) involves fraud against revenue or other
government functions. Therefore, based on the court record and the foregoing
analysis, it is the judgment of a majority of the members of the Committee
on Jurisprudence that the member pled guilty to a crime of moral turpitude before a federal court. Accordingly, the member has been automatically
expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry pursuant to Section

from all the rights and privileges of Masonry pursuant to Section 1404.820 of

Therefore, based on the court record and the foregoing analysis, it is the judgment of a majority of the members of the Committee on Jurisprudence that
the member pled guilty/no contest to a crime of moral turpitude before a state
court. Accordingly, the member has been automatically expelled from all the

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON TRIAL REVIEW

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Brethren, your Committee on Trial Review is required to adhere to
specific timelines. This year several cases were received by this committee in May for recommendation for appointment of Trial Masters which
did not permit sufficient time to perform all the tasks as required 45 days
before the Annual Communication. Consequently, filing charges after
April may well result in the matter not being heard by Grand Lodge in the
same year.
The Committee on Trial Review has carefully examined the records of
all cases completed during this Masonic year. In each matters the committee finds that there was compliance with the procedural requirements of the
California Masonic Code and in the findings of facts and where the accused
was found guilty the acts constituted un-Masonic conduct. The findings were
supported by the evidence. All references to the California Masonic Code are
abbreviated to “CMC.”
The following cases were decided by Trial Masters after investigation either because the accused failed to submit a plea or submitted
a plea of guilty or no contest:
1.

In Case Number 2811, one committee member recused himself from
the matter. The accused was charged and plead guilty during the Trial
Master’s investigation to the intentional infliction of physical and
mental injury and humiliation of a blindfolded candidate while in the
preparation room. The candidate’s pain was so severe that he fell to
his knees. The Trial Master found the accused guilty and fixed the
penalty at expulsion.

2.

In Case Number 2856, the accused was charged with sexually soliciting
a Masonic Brother’s wife via cell phone and texts using vile, indecent,
and profane language as well as photographs of himself in indecent
poses. The accused failed to respond. After investigation, the Trial

280

Proceedings of the

Master found the accused guilty with no mitigating circumstances and
fixed the penalty at expulsion. Documents filed after the decision of
the Trial Master were found to not constitute newly discovered evidence and thus not considered by the committee.
3.

In Case Number 2831, the accused, a suspended Mason since
2013, was charged with embezzlement. The accused falsely represented himself to be a Mason in good standing and was accepting
donations for the Shriners Hospital for Children while wearing a
Shriner’s Fez and Shirt. The accused was suspected of not turning
in all donated funds in the past. Based thereon, a marked $100 bill
was placed in the collection jar being carried by the accused which
was videoed. He did not turn in the $100 bill. The Trial Master
found the accused guilty of conduct involving moral turpitude
with aggravating circumstances and fixed the penalty at expulsion.
Documents filed after the decision of the Trial Master were found
to not constitute newly discovered evidence and thus not considered by the committee.

4.

In Case Numbers 2843 and 2844, each accused was charged with
knowingly holding membership in the same unrecognized lodge.
In Case Number 2844, the Trial Master found the accused started
his own Grand Lodge in California which included women Masons
and declared himself to be Grand Master. He solicited other regular Masons to join his Grand Lodge. In Case Number 2843, the
Trial Master found the accused joined this irregular lodge, had been
appointed by the accused in Case Number 2844 as a Master of the
Lodge of Perfection (14th Degree), and a member of the Supreme
Council of the 33rd Degree within the unrecognized Grand Lodge
jurisdiction. Neither resigned from the irregular lodge. In both cases,
the accused failed to respond to the charges, and the Trial Master
fixed the penalty for both at expulsion.
The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves
for the adoption of the following Resolution: “Resolved, that in Case
Numbers 2811, 2856, 2831, 2843 and 2844, the Trial Masters’ procedure, findings, and penalties affixed be hereby affirmed.”

5.

In Case Number 2821, the accused initially plead “not guilty” to the
charge of soliciting sexual intercourse and lewd acts with others
in exchange for money or other compensation. He subsequently
refused to proceed with a trial and agreed to investigation by the
Trial Master. After investigation, the Trial Master found that the
accused had invited the victim to a restaurant on the pretense
of acting as her mentor in a Masonic-affiliated organization. The

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

accused proceeded to loudly solicit sex from the victim and represented that she could make money attending Masonic events and
offering sexual favors. The Trial Master found the accused guilty
and that the conduct constituted moral turpitude and affixed the
penalty at expulsion.
The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves
for the adoption of the following resolution: “Resolved that in case
number 2821 the Trial Master’s procedures, findings and penalty
affixed be hereby affirmed.”
The following cases involved trial proceedings by the Trial Master
including the taking of testimony:
6.

In Case Number 2837, the Accused was charged with breach of his
fiduciary duty as Treasurer of the hall association as well as failing
in his duty as a Mason to conduct himself in a civil manner. As to
the first charge, the Trial Master found that the accused failed to pay
thousands of dollars in past due bills and refused to take responsibility. As to the second charge, the Trial Master found that when
confronted the accused not only denied accountability but expressed
anger and yelled at the members of his lodge. The Trial Master found
the accused guilty on both counts and fixed the penalty at a 6-month
definite suspension.

7.

In Case Number 2810, two committee members recused themselves.
The accused was charged with breaking a promise, trust, or confidence by falsehood and deceit. The accused, a licensed real estate
broker, allegedly represented to the accuser that he could help him
reduce his increasing monthly mortgage payments. The accused
arranged with the lender for a “short sale” of his home. The accuser
signed a Grant Deed and initialed a sales agreement to the accused’s
son as well as initialing a lease to the accused’s son. The accuser
insisted that he believed that the transaction was only a loan modification and that he continued to own the property. After the accuser
had paid rent to the son for 3 years, a dispute erupted between them.
The son filed an unlawful detainer proceeding against the accuser
who vacated the premises. The Trial Master concluded that the transaction was not a loan modification and that the accuser did not own
the property. The Trial Master further found that this was a business
dispute not involving fraud which under the CMC would not constitute un-Masonic conduct. The Trial Master accordingly found that
the accuser had failed to prove his case by a preponderance of the
evidence and therefore, the accused was not guilty.

282

Proceedings of the

8.

In the consolidated Case Numbers 2836 and 2839, the accused were
charged with refusing to obey the proper orders of the Master as
well as using abusive, vile, and profane language. The Trial Master
found the accusers failed to submit sufficient evidence that the
conduct had ever occurred. Accordingly, the Trial Master found
both accused not guilty.
The Committee on Trial Review submits and moves for the
adoption of the following Resolution: “Resolved that in Case
Numbers 2810, 2836, 2837, and 2839, the Trial Masters’ procedures,

The following case involved a trial proceeding with Commissioners
and the taking of testimony:
9.

In Case Number 2815, the accused was found guilty of a pattern of
un-Masonic conduct involving moral turpitude of harassing, defaming, spreading falsehoods, and using profane language in referring to
the mother of a Master Mason. The evidence included voice mails
of this conduct. The accused exhibited no remorse. The penalty was
fixed at a 90-day suspension. Documents filed after the decision of
the Trial Master were found to not constitute newly discovered evidence and thus not considered by the Committee.
The Trial Review Committee submits and moves for the adoption of the following resolution: “Resolved that in Case Number 2815
the Trial Master and Commissioners’ procedures, findings, verdict
and the penalty affixed be hereby affirmed.”

The following case was settled by the parties with the approval of the
Trial Master:
10. In Case No. 2855, the accused was charged with breach of fiduciary
duties as well as failing to obtain approval of the Masonic Properties
Committee before proceeding with the sale of the lodge building.
Prior to the lodge’s decision to sell the building due to significant
financial conditions, the hall association had lost its tax-exempt
status. Accordingly, the sale of the building before resolving the
tax-exempt status of the hall association could subject it and the
lodge to substantial tax liability from the sale of the building. Had
the accused complied with the Code, the loss of the hall association’s
tax-exempt status might have been discovered and the potential
tax liability avoided. The accused eventually pleaded guilty to the
charges, and the parties negotiated a settlement agreement with
terms acceptable to the Trial Master. As part of the settlement, the
accused accepted a penalty of 3 months suspension, agreed that he

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

would not serve as an elected officer of any constituent lodge or
building association for a period of 18 months, and agreed to a potential enhancement of the suspension by an additional 9 months should
the tax liability be imposed. It is the opinion of the Committee on
Trial Review that the conditional enhancement of the fixed suspension of the penalty is unenforceable and, therefore, recommends that
the penalty be affirmed except that the period of suspension be set at
a fixed period of six months.
The Committee on Trial Review submits and moves for the
adoption of the following resolution: “Resolved that in Case Number
2855 the Trial Master’s procedures, findings and penalty be affirmed
except that the suspension be set at a fixed period of 6 months.”
The following cases had Trial Masters appointed but did not proceed
to findings. Nonetheless, these cases require Grand Lodge action:
11. In Case Number 2841, the charges were received under Chapter 4 of
the CMC by the Committee on Trial Review in November of 2018.
Shortly thereafter, the accused became Master of a Lodge. Charges
against a sitting Master can only proceed under the provisions of
CMC Chapter 3 which are substantially different than the procedures to be applied to a Mason under CMC Chapter 4. Accordingly,
the Committee on Trial Review has found that it has no jurisdiction
to proceed and has recommended that the charges be dismissed
without prejudice subject to refiling in the future at the option of
the accuser.
The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves
the adoption of the following resolution: “Resolved that Case
Number 2841 be dismissed without prejudice.”
12. In Case Number 2838, the accused died before the Trial Master could
complete his investigation or make findings. As a result, the deceased
is no longer subject to the jurisdiction of the Trial Review Committee
or the Grand Lodge.
The Committee on Trial Review submits and moves the adoption of the following resolution: Resolved that Case Number 2838 be
dismissed.”
The following cases involved previously expelled members who have
requested restoration of Masonic membership:
13. In Cases 2737 and 2738, the matters are factually linked. Both Mr.
Conrado Montero and Mr. Aldrin Reyes were expelled in 2016.
While acting as Stewards in the preparation room during a Degree,

283

284

Proceedings of the

the candidate was hoodwinked, and subsequently battered. The
Trial Master found that Reyes battered the candidate despite his
denials and that Montero lied about Reyes’ presence in the preparation room. There was no finding by the Trial Master that Montero
battered the candidate. In 2017 and 2018, the Grand Lodge denied
both of their requests for reinstatement. Their current requests are
different than previously submitted. In this application their lodge
unanimously voted to recommend their restoration. Both sent letters
of apology to the victim. Each has undertaken rehabilitative efforts
towards the lodge and the community. However, only 3 years have
elapsed since the expulsion. Reyes, who was found to have committed the battery, refers in his apology to his acts as “negligent” rather
than intentional, leading one to question the sincerity of his apology. He needs to understand he was not expelled for negligence, but
for committing a criminal battery. The candidate had entrusted his
well-being to our care during his initiation. The candidate testified
that Reyes told him later to “take it like a man, get over it and move
on, you can get the next candidate.”
In contrast, the Trial Master found that Montero’s actions consisted of less serious conduct. It also is the opinion of the Committee
that Montero repeatedly demonstrated his remorse for his less serious conduct and sincerely expressed his apologies.
The Committee on Trial Review submits and moves the adoption of the following resolution: “Resolved that in Case Number 2738
as to Mr. Montero, his application for reinstatement be granted.”
The Committee on Trial Review submits and moves the adoption of the following resolution: “Resolved that in Case Number 2737
as to Mr. Reyes, his application for reinstatement be denied.”

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON YOUTH ORDERS

To the Most Worshipful Grand Master, Stuart A. Wright, and the members of the
Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of California:
We all agree that the youth of today are our future. We can also concur
that the world needs the values that our Masonic family shares. California
Freemasonry has long realized that by fostering the development and growth
of the three Masonic Youth Orders (Job’s Daughters, Rainbow and DeMolay),
we are improving our world.
Your Grand Lodge Committee on Youth Orders is charged with ensuring
that our lodges and members continue to support our youth orders by providing the necessary leadership and assistance to aid in their success.
Following a long-term strategic plan, the Committee is focusing on:
• Supporting our three Masonic Youth Orders, their members,

and advisors

• Serving as a liaison between our Youth Orders and Masonry
• Encouraging and developing Youth Orders advisors within the

family of Freemasonry

• Recognizing exemplary performance.

In order to accomplish these objectives, we have divided the committee
into seven task forces, and we are already seeing results.
This year, we invited alumni from each of our four youth orders to participate on the committee. While they don’t carry a vote, the input and effort from
these young adults has proven very valuable. We thank Christina Dunbar and
Raisa Beckford of Job’s Daughters, and Max Shoemaker of SoCal DeMolay for
participating so fully this past year. We look forward to welcoming immediate
Past NorCal DeMolay Master Councilor Brett Grimm, as well as a representative from Rainbow for Girls this next year.
We have increased our coordination with the Masonic Center for Youth

286

Proceedings of the

and Families (MCYAF) and our youth orders. Thanks to Kimberly Rich and Dr.
Sheening Lin, we are providing the youth and their advisors with tools to cope
with many of the world’s challenges, including bullying, stress management,
and depression and anxiety.
The committee again embraced its role as the facilitator of the Masonic
Adult Youth Orders (MAYO) meetings throughout the year. These meetings
are attended and supported by the leadership of the York Rite and Scottish
Rite bodies, Eastern Star and Amaranth.
Grand Master’s Youth Order Support Award
The Youth Orders Committee was pleased to recommend the names of
the following brethren to receive the Grand Master’s Youth Support Award:
• Worshipful Brother Robert D. Alexander of Simi Valley Lodge

No. 806

• Brother Mark C. Read of Oceanside San Dieguito Lodge No. 381
• Brother Geoffrey B. Matlack of Bellflower Lodge No. 320
• Brother Jon A. Harris of Liberty Lodge No. 299

Each was selected by the Grand Master to receive the award in recognition of his outstanding commitment and service to our Masonic youth and
was so honored during the Public Ceremonies of Annual Communication on
Sunday, October 20, 2019.
The committee was very involved in the centennial celebrations for
DeMolay during 2019. Very Worshipful Brother Glenn Woody chaired the
centennial planning committee. Among the highlights were the nearly 200
Brother Masons who received “honorary” DeMolay degrees throughout
the state.
In addition, Avery Brinkley, Past Master Councilor of SoCal DeMolay, completed his term as International Master Councilor of DeMolay International in
June. There is no doubt he made a difference for the Order in his many travels
across the globe.
We look forward to supporting Job’s Daughters as they observe their centennial in 2021, and Rainbow for Girls in 2022. These are terrific opportunities
to celebrate our accomplishments and share the good works of each order
with the public.
The committee members are grateful to each of the adult leaders of our
California Youth Orders, who continue to provide the leadership and mentorship that has elevated the California Youth Orders to the top of their respective international organizations.

The members of the committee are appreciative of the confidence placed
in us by Most Worshipful Wright and look forward to working closely with Most
Worshipful Trauner and the rest of the Grand Lodge Executive Committee.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
CALIFORNIA FREEMASON

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
This committee is honored to have had the opportunity to provide guidance and direction for California Freemason magazine, the flagship publication
of our Grand Lodge. This year’s issues raised topics that appeal to our broad
audience and resonate with members far and wide. The California Freemason
magazine is delivered bi-monthly to over 42,000 members and over 14,000
widows.
• November/December 2018: Friendship: The Bonds of a Lifelong

Brotherhood

• January/February 2019: 2018 Annual Report focus on lodge giving

to the Let’s Write the Future Campaign

• March/April 2019: 100 Years of DeMolay International—

A Celebration of the Centennial

• May/June 2019: Of Their Own Free Will and Accord: Women

and Freemasonry

• July/August 2019: The Outdoors Issue: Masons in the Great Outdoors
• September/October 2019: Crafting their Legacy: Masonic Folk Art

in California and Beyond

Early this year, we launched californiafreemason.org, our new home on
the web. This new website is easy to read and share, and easy to search.
Stories from the magazine are more connected and better archived to help
facilitate a deeper consideration of many of the topics that are important to
our Brethren.
We are very pleased to report that in June 2019, California Freemason was
commended once again by the Association of Membership Publishers EXCEL
Awards. More than 800 entries were received in dozens of award categories; of

Bronze Award, Best Single-Topic Issue: Sacred Geometry

RECOGNITION OF
FOREIGN GRAND LODGES 2019
The Grand Lodge of California recognizes all of the grand lodges in
the United States published in the 2019 List of Lodges Masonic, which includes
all 50 states and the District of Columbia. In addition, the Grand Lodge of
California recognizes a number of Prince Hall grand lodges and foreign grand
lodges around the world. The Grand Lodge of California recognizes some, but
not all, of the foreign grand lodges in the 2019 List of Lodges Masonic as well as
a number of foreign grand lodges that are not listed therein.
For clarity, the foreign grand lodges that are recognized by the Grand
Lodge of California are listed below alphabetically by country. For those
that are published in the 2019 List of Lodges Masonic, the corresponding page
number is provided in parentheses. Recognized grand lodges that are not published in the 2019 List of Lodges Masonic are marked with an asterisk (*). The
Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of California is responsible for all correspondence with these grand lodges and the lodges under their jurisdiction.
Please contact this office for assistance.

PRINCE HALL GRAND LODGES
The Grand Lodge of California has mutual recognition with a number of
Prince Hall grand lodges in the United States. In addition, the Grand Lodge of
California has extended an offer of recognition to a number of Prince Hall grand
lodges throughout the country where mutual recognition does not yet exist.
The Grand Lodge of California maintains mutual recognition with the following Prince Hall grand lodges. For those that are published in the 2019 List
of Lodges Masonic, the corresponding page number is provided in parentheses. Recognized Prince Hall grand lodges that are not published in the 2019
List of Lodges Masonic are marked with an asterisk (*). The terms of recognition are the same with each Prince Hall grand lodge and are consistent with
the agreement of mutual recognition between the Grand Lodge of California
and the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California, Inc. Namely, dual membership
in lodges under the two jurisdictions is not allowed, but visitation may be had
between members of lodges of both jurisdictions. For these purposes, visitation means visiting tiled meetings.
ALASKA: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Alaska and Its Jurisdiction, Inc.
(20); ARIZONA: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Arizona and Its Jurisdiction*;
CALIFORNIA: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California, Inc. (27); COLORADO
(Wyoming and Utah): Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Colorado, Wyoming and
Utah*, CONNECTICUT: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Connecticut, Inc.
(29); DELAWARE: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Delaware (32); DISTRICT
OF COLUMBIA: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of the District of Columbia
(includes lodges in Maryland) (34) ; ILLINOIS: Prince Hall Grand Lodge
of Illinois (46); MARYLAND: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Maryland and Its
Jurisdiction*; MASSACHUSETTS (Maine and New Hampshire): Prince
Hall Grand Lodge Jurisdiction of Massachusetts*; MISSOURI: Prince Hall
Grand Lodge of Missouri and Jurisdiction*; NEBRASKA: Prince Hall Grand
Lodge of Nebraska and Its Jurisdiction*; NEVADA: Prince Hall Grand Lodge
of Nevada and Jurisdiction, Inc.*; NEW MEXICO: Prince Hall Grand Lodge
of the State of New Mexico, Inc.*; OREGON (Idaho and Montana): Prince

of Canada in the Province of Ontario*, PENNSYLVANIA: Prince Hall Grand
Lodge Jurisdiction of Pennsylvania* (includes lodges in Ohio); TEXAS: Prince
Hall Grand Lodge Jurisdiction of Texas (112).

Report of Independent Auditors
To the Board of Trustees
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California
Report on Consolidated Financial Statements
We have audited the accompanying consolidated financial statements of The Most Worshipful Grand
Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California (the “Grand Lodge”), which comprise
the consolidated statement of financial position as of October 31, 2019, and the related consolidated
statements of activities and changes in net assets, and cash flows for the year then ended, and the
related notes to the consolidated financial statements.
Management’s Responsibility for the Consolidated Financial Statements

Management is responsible for the preparation and fair presentation of these consolidated financial
statements in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of
America; this includes the design, implementation, and maintenance of internal control relevant to the
preparation and fair presentation of consolidated financial statements that are free from material
misstatement, whether due to fraud or error.
Auditor’s Responsibility

Our responsibility is to express an opinion on these consolidated financial statements based on our
audit. We conducted our audit in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the United
States of America. Those standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable
assurance about whether the consolidated financial statements are free from material misstatement.
An audit involves performing procedures to obtain audit evidence about the amounts and disclosures
in the consolidated financial statements. The procedures selected depend on the auditor’s judgment,
including the assessment of the risks of material misstatement of the consolidated financial statements,
whether due to fraud or error. In making those risk assessments, the auditor considers internal control
relevant to the entity’s preparation and fair presentation of the consolidated financial statements in
order to design audit procedures that are appropriate in the circumstances, but not for the purpose of
expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of the entity’s internal control. Accordingly, we express no
such opinion. An audit also includes evaluating the appropriateness of accounting policies used and
the reasonableness of significant accounting estimates made by management, as well as evaluating
the overall presentation of the consolidated financial statements.
We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis
for our audit opinion.

1

426

Proceedings of the

Opinion

In our opinion, the consolidated financial statements referred to above present fairly, in all material
respects, the financial position of The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of
the State of California as of October 31, 2019, and the changes in its net assets and its cash flows for
the year then ended in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States
of America.
Emphasis of a Matter

As discussed in Note 1 to the consolidated financial statements, the Organization adopted Financial
Accounting Standards Board (“FASB”) Accounting Standards Update (“ASU”) No. 2016-14, Not-forProfit Entities (Topic 958): Presentation of Financial Statements of Not-for-Profit Entities. The adoption
of the standard resulted in additional footnote disclosures and changes to the classification of net
assets and the disclosures related to net assets. The ASU has been applied retrospectively to all
periods presented with the exception of the omission of certain information as permitted by the ASU.
Our opinion is not modified with respect to this matter.
Other Matters
Report on Summarized Comparative Information

We have previously audited the Grand Lodge’s 2018 consolidated financial statements and we
expressed an unmodified opinion on those audited consolidated financial statements in our report dated
March 23, 2019. In our opinion, the summarized comparative information presented herein as of and
for the year ended October 31, 2018, is consistent, in all material respects, with the audited
consolidated financial statements, from which it has been derived.
Supplementary Information

Our audit was conducted for the purpose of forming an opinion on the consolidated financial statements
as a whole. The accompanying consolidating statement of financial position, consolidating statement
of activities and changes in net assets, and consolidating schedule of changes in net assets as of and
for the year ended October 31, 2019, are presented for purposes of additional analysis and are not a
required part of the consolidated financial statements. Such information is the responsibility of
management and was derived from and relates directly to the underlying accounting and other records
used to prepare the consolidated financial statements. Such information has been subjected to the
auditing procedures applied in the audit of the consolidated financial statements and certain additional
procedures, including comparing and reconciling such information directly to the underlying accounting
and other records used to prepare the consolidated financial statements or to the consolidated financial
statements themselves, and other additional procedures in accordance with auditing standards
generally accepted in the United States of America. In our opinion, the information is fairly stated in all
material respects in relation to the consolidated financial statements as a whole.

Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California

Other Information

Our audit was conducted for the purpose of forming an opinion on the basic financial statements as a
whole. The accompanying schedule of fraternal expenses, schedule of program appropriations, and
schedule of general and administrative expenses for the years ended October 31, 2019 and 2018, all
presented as supplementary information, are presented for purposes of additional analysis and are not
a required part of the basic consolidated financial statements. Such information has not been subjected
to the auditing procedures applied in the audit of the basic consolidated financial statements, and
accordingly, we do not express an opinion or provide any assurance on it.

NOTE 1 – SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES
History and organization – The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of
California (the “Grand Lodge”) is a nonprofit, unincorporated fraternal organization governed by a constitution and
ordinances setting forth its jurisdiction and authority. The jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge includes all lodges and
Masons within the state of California, and members of lodges of California, wherever residing.
The Grand Lodge provides general and administrative services to its related entities: The Masonic Homes of
California (the “Masonic Homes”) and its subsidiary Acacia Creek, a Senior Living Retirement Community in Union
City (“Acacia Creek Union City”); the California Masonic Memorial Temple (the “Temple”); and the California
Masonic Foundation (the “Foundation”) (collectively, the “Masonic Entities”). These services are reimbursed by the
related entities.
The California Masonic Code (“Code”) sets forth the effects and process of a lodge dissolution upon the surrender
of its charter. The members of the chartered lodges of the Sublime Benicia Lodge No. 5, Plumas Lodge No. 60,
Foothill Lodge No. 305, Moreno Valley Lodge No. 804, and Pomona Valley Lodge No. 246, voted to surrender their
respective charters to the Grand Lodge. The Grand Lodge accepted the surrender of these lodges’ charters and
directed that these lodges be dissolved in accordance with the Code.
Upon the surrender of a lodge charter, Grand Lodge assumes the position of the lodge and becomes the sole
member of the lodge’s Hall Association. As a result of the lodges’ dissolution named above, the Grand Lodge
became the sole member of the following Hall Associations:
x

The Benicia Masonic Temple Association (“Benicia Hall”) on October 11, 2014;

x

Plumas Hall Association (“Plumas Hall”) on October 10, 2015;

x

Monrovia Masonic Building Association (“Monrovia Hall”) on October 10, 2015;

x

King Solomon’s Moreno Valley Temple Association (“Moreno Valley Hall”) on October 28, 2016; and

x

Pomona Valley Masonic Temple Association (“Pomona Valley”) on February 7, 2018.

The financial statements of these “Hall Associations” are included in the consolidated financial statements of the
Grand Lodge.
Principles of consolidation – The consolidated financial statements include accounts of the Grand Lodge, Nob
Hill, and the Hall Associations (collectively, the “Organization”). All significant inter-company accounts and
transactions have been eliminated.
Comparative information – The consolidated financial statements include certain prior year summarized
comparative information in total but not by net asset class. Such information does not include sufficient detail to
constitute a presentation in conformity with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of
America. Accordingly, such information should be read in conjunction with the Organization’s consolidated financial
statements for the year ended October 31, 2018, from which the summarized information was derived.

Net assets classifications – The accompanying consolidated financial statements have been prepared in
accordance with the standards set forth in Financial Accounting Standards Board (“FASB”) Accounting Standards
Codification (“ASC”) 958-605 Revenue Recognition, ASC 958-205 Presentation of Financial Statements, and the
guidelines set forth in the industry audit and accounting guide Not-for-Profit Entities issued by the American Institute
of Certified Public Accountants. Under these guidelines, contributions of cash and other assets are classified as
one of the following three categories:
Without Donor Restrictions – Net assets without donor restrictions represent resources that are not subject to
donor-imposed stipulations and are available to support all activities of the Grand Lodge, including the Grand
Lodge Endowment Fund (the “Endowment Fund”).
At the 2018 Annual Communication, the Charter of Pomona Valley No. 246 was revoked and all assets were
transferred to Grand Lodge for future lodges. No such transfers of assets occurred at the 2019 Annual
Communication.
The Endowment Fund was established at the Grand Lodge’s October 1993, Annual Communication. If, in any
fiscal year, there was an excess of support and revenues over expenses, as defined by the Grand Lodge
Executive Committee, the excess shall be added to the Endowment Fund. For the years ended October 31,
2019 and 2018, excess of support and revenues over expenses are $41,073 and $93,432, respectively.
With Donor restrictions – Net assets with donor restrictions represent contributions that are limited in use in
accordance with donor-imposed stipulations. These stipulations may expire with time and/or may be satisfied
by the actions of the Grand Lodge according to the intention of the donor. Upon satisfaction of such stipulations,
the associated net assets are released from net assets with donor restrictions and reported as net assets
without donor restrictions.
Use of estimates – The preparation of consolidated financial statements in conformity with accounting principles
generally accepted in the United States of America requires management to make estimates and assumptions.
These estimates and assumptions affect the reported amounts of assets and liabilities, disclosure of contingent
assets and liabilities at the date of the consolidated financial statements, and the reported amounts of revenues
and expenses during the reporting period. Actual results could differ from those estimates.
Fair value of financial instruments – The carrying amounts reported in the accompanying consolidated
statements of financial position for cash and cash equivalents, accounts receivable, accounts payable and accrued
liabilities, and due from/due to related entities, approximate fair value due to their short-term nature. Discussion on
the fair value of financial instruments is included in Note 2.

Fair value process – The Organization determines fair value measurement policies and procedures for assets and
liabilities under the supervision of the Investment Committee. These policies and procedures are reassessed
annually to determine if the current valuation techniques are still appropriate. A variety of qualitative factors are
used to subjectively determine the most appropriate valuation methodologies. Methodologies are consistent with
market, income, and cost approaches. Unobservable inputs used in fair value measurements are evaluated and
adjusted on an annual basis, or as necessary based on current market conditions and other third party information.
In determining the reasonableness of the methodology, Grand Lodge evaluates a variety of factors including a
review of existing agreements, economic conditions, industry, and market developments. Certain unobservable
inputs are assessed through review of contract terms while others are substantiated utilizing available market data
including, but not limited to, market comparable, qualified opinions, and discount rates and mortality tables for split
interest agreements.
Cash and cash equivalents – Cash and cash equivalents consist of highly liquid investments with original
maturities of three months or less at the time of purchase, with the exception of cash and cash equivalents held as
investments.
Prepaid expenses – Prepaid expenses consist primarily of prepaid insurance coverage.
Investments – Investments in fixed income and equity securities are stated at estimated fair values based on
quoted market prices. Investments received through gifts are recorded at estimated fair values at the date of
donation. The fair value of alternative investments is recorded at the investment manager’s Net Asset Value
(“NAV”), as the managers have the greatest insight into the investments of their funds and the related industry and
have the appropriate expertise to determine the NAV. The Grand Lodge assesses the NAV and takes into
consideration events such as suspended redemptions, restructuring, secondary sales, and investor defaults to
determine if an adjustment is necessary. Additionally, asset holdings are reviewed within the investment manager’s
audited financial statements, as are interim financial statements and fund manager communications, for the
purposes of assessing valuation. Unrealized gains or losses that result from market fluctuations are recorded in the
period in which such fluctuations occur. Realized gains or losses resulting from sales or maturities of securities are
calculated on a cost basis.
Property and equipment – Property and equipment, including leasehold improvements, greater than $1,000 are
recorded at cost and are depreciated using the straight-line method over estimated useful lives of 3 to 25 years.
The Grand Lodge periodically evaluates the carrying value of its long-lived assets for impairment. The evaluations
address the estimated recoverability of the assets’ carrying value, which is principally determined based on
projected undiscounted cash flows generated by the underlying tangible assets. When the carrying value of an
asset exceeds its estimated recoverability, a write-down is recorded. No impairment was recorded during the years
ended October 31, 2019 and 2018.
Other assets – Other assets consist primarily of a collection of jewelry used in lodge ceremonies.
Deferred per capita dues revenue – Deferred per capita dues revenue consists of dues received in the current
year for the subsequent fiscal year. These amounts are recognized as revenue using the straight-line method over
the period to which they relate.

Assets held in trust for lodges life membership and general master trust funds – Assets held in trust for
lodges general master trust fund consists of lodges’ participation in the Grand Lodge’s investment pool. The assets
held in trust for lodges life membership fund is held in Kaspick and invested in the Kaspick & Company Growth
Income Fund. Investments are held and managed by the Grand Lodge.
Revenue recognition – Contributions are recognized as revenue when received or unconditionally promised.
Noncash donations are recognized at fair value at the time of the donation. Garage revenues are recognized when
earned as services are provided. Program service revenues are recognized when received and in the period to
which they relate. Dues are recognized as revenue ratably over the period to which they relate.
Concentration of credit risk – Financial instruments potentially subjecting the Grand Lodge to concentrations of
credit risk consist primarily of bank demand deposits in excess of Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (“FDIC”)
insurance thresholds, cash held in money market accounts in excess of the amounts insured by the U.S. Treasury
insurance for money market funds, and various debt and equity investments in excess of Securities Investor
Protection Corporation (“SIPC”) insurance. Demand deposits are placed with a local financial institution, and
management has not experienced any loss related to these demand deposits in the past. Investment securities are
exposed to various risks, such as interest rate, market, and credit risk. It is at least reasonably possible, given the
level of risk associated with investment securities, that changes in the near term could materially affect the amount
reported in the consolidated statements. The risk associated with the investments is mitigated through
diversification.
Income tax status – The Grand Lodge has been granted tax-exempt status for both federal income and California
franchise tax purposes; while Nob Hill, a subsidiary of the Grand Lodge, is subject to federal income and California
franchise tax.
New accounting pronouncements – During 2019, the Organization adopted FASB ASU No. 2016-14, Not-forProfit Entities (Topic 958): Presentation of Financial Statements of Not-for-Profit Entities. This guidance is intended
to improve the net asset classification requirements and the information presented in consolidated financial
statements and notes about an entity’s liquidity, financial performance, and cash flows. Main provisions of this
guidance include: presentation of two classes of net assets versus the previously required three; recognition of
capital gifts for construction as a net asset without donor restrictions when the associated long-lived asset is placed
in service; recognition of underwater endowment funds as a reduction in net assets with donor restrictions; and
reporting investment income net of external and direct internal investment expenses. The guidance also enhances
disclosures for board designated amounts, compositions of net assets with donor restrictions and how the
restrictions affect the use of resources, qualitative and quantitative information about the liquidity and availability of
financial assets to meet general expenditures within one year of the statement of financial position date, and
expenses by both their natural and functional classification, including methods used to allocate costs among
program and support functions and underwater endowments.

ASC 820, Fair Value Measurements and Disclosures, defines fair value as the price that would be received to sell
an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement
date. ASC 820 also establishes a fair value hierarchy that requires an entity to maximize the use of observable
inputs and minimize the use of unobservable inputs when measuring fair value. The standard describes three levels
of inputs that may be used to measure fair value:
Level 1 – Quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities.
Level 2 – Observable inputs other than Level 1 prices, such as quoted prices for similar assets or liabilities;
quoted prices in markets that are not active; or other inputs that are observable or can be
corroborated by observable market data for substantially the full term of the assets or liabilities; or
net asset value (NAV) per share (or its equivalent) with the ability to redeem the investments in the
near term.
Level 3 – Unobservable inputs that are supported by little or no market activity and that are significant to the
fair value of the assets or liabilities.

Following is a description of the valuation methodology used for instruments measured at fair value on a recurring
basis and recognized in the accompanying consolidated financial statements, as well as the general classification
of such instruments pursuant to the valuation hierarchy:
Investments – Where quoted market prices are available in an active market, securities are classified within
Level 1 of the valuation hierarchy. Level 1 securities include exchange traded equities. If quoted market prices
are not available, then fair values are estimated by using pricing models, quoted prices of securities with
identical characteristics, or discounted cash flows. In certain cases, where Level 1 or Level 2 inputs are not
available, securities are classified within Level 3 of the hierarchy and include certain real estate investments,
and other less liquid securities using investment appropriate models like the income approach for real estate
investments.

Foreign stocks – This represents an investment in Acadian Non-US All Cap Equity (USD Hedged) Fund. The
fund’s objective is to seek long-term capital appreciation in investing primarily in common stocks of international
issuers. This will include both large and small-cap issuers as well as opportunistic exposure to issuers in the
emerging markets. Acadian uses a quantitative model to invest in all cap international value equity.
Domestic equity – These common trust funds are invested and reinvested primarily in a portfolio of equity securities
with the objective of approximating as closely as practicable the capitalization weighted total rate of return of the
entire United States market for publicly traded equity securities. The criterion for selection of investments is the Dow
Jones U.S. Total Stock Market Index.
Foreign equity – This category represents investments in Global Equity Long-Only Fund LP, formerly known as
Fiera USA Global Equities Fund LP, and Hexavest Global Equity Fund.
The Global Equity Long-Only Fund LP’s investment objective is to invest primarily in long-only portfolio of global
equities. The Hexavest Global Equity Fund’s investment objective is to provide investors with capital appreciation,
and or income generated from investments in securities of issuers located in developed market countries. The
investments are spread across global markets, and the objective of the underlying funds is to provide investors with
capital appreciation and dividend income, while charging a lower expense fee than traditional mutual funds.
Alternative investments
Real Estate (“UBS TPF”) – This is an investment in an actively managed core portfolio of equity real estate that
seeks to provide attractive returns while limiting downside risk and has both relative and real return objectives.
Its relative performance objective is to outperform the NFI-ODCE index over any given three-to-five year period.
The fund’s real return performance objective is to achieve at least a 5% real rate of return (i.e., inflation-adjusted
return), before advisory fees, over any given three-to-five year period.
